title: AI data centres to self-administer funds in Tasmanian community deal
text:
Tasmanian data centre proponents would each run their own community benefit funds under a proposal from the state government.

Premier Jeremy Rockliff announced his government's statement of expectations for data centres on Friday, which includes rules for the community funds.

Once a facility is operational, proponents would be required to pay into their own funds, at a rate of $3,000 per megawatt (MW) of contracted energy each year.

The requirement to pay into community funds is included in the Tasmanian government's statement of expectations. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

For Tasmania's largest AI data centre company, Firmus, its 104MW facility at St Leonards would contribute $312,000 per year.

It also has a proposed 288MW centre planned for Long Reach, near Bell Bay, and a 40MW centre at Wesley Vale in the state's north-west.

Last month, Premier Rockliff announced plans for a singular local community benefit fund, but did not release the cost or structure.

Jeremy Rockliff (left) has since released more details about the community funds that would impact companies such as Tim Rosenfield's (centre) and Oliver Curtis' Firmus. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

At Friday's press conference, further details were announced.

The premier and Industry Minister Felix Ellis spoke of a single fund governed by "local people" and "local representatives" who would allocate grants to "community groups and other eligible organisations".

They did not reveal that there would be several funds or that companies themselves would control the funds.

The statement of expectations outlines "transparent governance arrangements" and requires public reporting.

Greens MP Tabatha Badger said she was "very curious" about how the community funds would be run.

"How do Tasmanians have the confidence that these companies are actually going to fairly engage with them and invest in the things that matter to Tasmanians?" she said.

Expectations to be binding

Premier Rockliff announced plans for the fund in the days following Firmus's scrapped IPO, which unravelled due to investor concerns about the company's finances, expansion plans and social licence.

He said today that the expectations document would be reviewed within six months.

"In our view, [data centres] are a good investment for Tasmania and we welcome that investment," Mr Rockliff said.

" But the guardrails are important, particularly when it comes to community expectations, when it comes to transparency and when it comes to investing back in the local community. "

Six new data centre proposals for Tasmania, but companies not named Unnamed companies are looking at setting up six data centres in Tasmania, a parliamentary document reveals.

Mr Ellis said proponents who did not follow the expectations "won't be able to proceed".

"There are already many statutory rules that the data centre developers are required to meet in areas such as planning and environmental requirements," he said.

The state government has been under pressure to step up its regulation of the burgeoning sector, following Firmus unveiling plans for multiple data centres in the state.

Opponents to data centres have raised concerns about where the energy and water used by the AI data factories will come from.

Proposals for AI data centres in Tasmania have been met with some local opposition. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

For the Firmus factory at St Leonards, state energy company Aurora has contracted energy supply through the initial stage, but it does not have a long-term deal.

Energy Minister Nick Duigan said proponents were "required" to partner with new renewable energy projects, but they could do that "through" Hydro Tasmania.

"So Hydro would go out and contract with the new renewable energy providers and act as an aggregator to provide a firmed energy product to the data centre," he said.

Industry backs fund

Russell Kelly, chief executive of technology sector advocate TasICT, said the expectations "put the onus" on data centre proponents to build trust with the community.

Russell Kelly says the fund will help AI data centre companies build trust. (ABC News: Cameron Atkins)

Mr Kelly said the amount proposed for the Local Community Benefit Fund was in line with other proposals in the nation.

"The tech sector can see this fund building benefits broader than the development itself," he said.

"We can see a pipeline of young Tasmanians getting jobs in technology. We can see closer association between the University of Tasmania and TasTAFE."

Fiona Turner of start-up hub Enterprize welcomed the expectations.

"Giving skills back to locals around AI is very important, especially with these data centres here," she said.

title: Salmon farm antibiotic use impact 'completely unfair' cray fisher says
text:
A commercial fisher says the impact of salmon companies' antibiotic use in Tasmania is "completely unfair" on smaller, wild fishers.

Kodey Rolston, who works as a deckhand on a cray fishing boat, said while he was a supporter of the salmon industry, "fishermen are being impacted so deeply by what salmon farming has done".

The Department of Natural Resources and Environment (NRE) is closing two commercial fishing areas from Sunday until February 14.

Commercial rock lobster fisheries closed due to antibiotic trade risk Commercial rock lobster and dive fisheries in parts of Tasmania's south-east will be closed for three months to "mitigate trade risks" linked to antibiotic use.

The commercial taking of rock lobster and the setting of rock lobster pots will not be allowed within parts of the Southern Channel "therapeutic management area" (TMA).

Commercial divers will not be allowed to take short-spined sea urchins, long-spined sea urchins and periwinkles in the Northern Channel TMA.

Under the state government's Aquaculture Therapeutant — Wild Fisheries Market Access Management Plan, released last month, wild fisheries near salmon pens treated with antibiotics get temporarily closed.

The closures are to protect export markets as some countries have zero tolerance for antibiotics in wild-caught fish.

The two new closures are linked to salmon company Tassal's recent use of the antibiotic oxytetracycline (OTC) at its salmon farms at Great Taylors Bay and Meads Creek in the lower D'Entrecasteaux Channel.

The company said the closure accounted for 1.6 per cent of the state's historical rock lobster catch.

A map showing the areas of the rock lobster fishery that will be closed from Sunday. (ABC News: Hamed Akrami)

But Mr Rolston said the closure area was "vital to the crayfishing industry".

"Down south is our safe haven for abalones, for crayfish.

"It's a multi, multi-generational fishing ground and it's being locked off all together because the salmon farms want to just dump as much antibiotics in the water as they can to try and save their own arse and not cooperate with other businesses," he said.

"I actually don't have anything against the salmon farms.

"In all honesty, I'm very much for them — they provide a lot of jobs all around the state.

" But when it starts interring with small fisheries, small businesses, and it's just one or two businesses ruining it for everyone else, it's completely unfair. "

Tassal says the rock lobster fishery closure accounts for 1.6 per cent of Tasmania's annual rock lobster catch. (ABC News: Bec Pridham)

Tasmanian Greens leader Rosalie Woodruff said the government was expecting the wild-caught fishing industry to "do all the heavy lifting".

"Wild fishers have been sidelined and the interests of big salmon companies have been put first by the government," Ms Woodruff said.

"They've refused to put in place any regulations to constrain the operations of salmon farming in the Channel."

'Important that all industries work together': Premier

Premier Jeremy Rockliff said it was important "we get the balance right".

"We value our wild fishery, we value our aquaculture industry and it's important that all sea industries coexist and coexist amongst the best balanced approach, which we are trying to achieve here," Mr Rockliff said.

"The industry is in a transition and a very quick transition in terms of antibiotic use because of the investment that's going into breeding, for example, will mean that in future years there'll be less reliance on antibiotics if at all, and that's the space we need to get to.

"We're in a transition time now and I know it's difficult … I feel for industry outside of the salmon industry very much.

"It's important that all industries work together, we get the balance right."

In a statement yesterday, Tassal said the closure was a "precaution to protect export market access".

"Public Health has confirmed swimming and recreational fishing remain completely safe.

"We recognise the consequences for any affected commercial rock lobster fishers and are working with the wild fisheries sector on appropriate support, with monitoring underway to support reopening as soon as possible."

Tassal has been administering OTC by injection, rather than orally through medicated food.

title: Outlook outage expected to cost Australian businesses billions of dollars
text:
The Microsoft outage is calculated to cost Australian businesses billions of dollars, with experts warning small businesses will be the hardest hit by the technology failure.

A widespread outage, which started about 3:15 am AEDT, has hit platforms including Outlook, with many users having trouble accessing emails and encountering errors across the Microsoft suite of products.

Workers across multiple types of businesses have reported being unable to access email or SharePoint, with some resorting to using fax machines to keep operating.

Microsoft outage live: For the latest on the issues impacting the tech giant's apps read our blog.

RSM Australia Risk Advisory partner Ashwin Pal said the cost to professional service businesses, such as lawyers or accountants, would be hundreds of thousands of dollars per hour.

"It's not just the initial downtime, it's more actually about then the catch up effort because that costs money," he said.

"Because now when things do normalise, you're going to have to spend money to actually catch up because of all the backlog."

Ashwin Pal says Monday's backlog of work will be costly. (Supplied)

He said the impact of the outage was amplified by the 3.9 million businesses globally that used the Microsoft suite, with many not having backup systems, resulting in huge costs to the economy.

"It's billions of dollars. And don't forget, it's actually going to get worse," he said.

"This is what happened with CrowdStrike. So when the outage happened, because of where we are in the world in terms of time zones, we felt the impact first.

"As the US and Europe come online, and they can't operate, it's going to get worse. So you're going to have a multiplier effect."

Outlook down as Microsoft outage hits Australians Microsoft says it has begun restoring access to its email and other online services after Australians experienced outages for several hours today.

He said the repercussions would be most keenly felt by small businesses, due to operating on thin margins.

"You take a CBA as an example, they'll be able to absorb an impact like this a lot easier than the five-person accounting shop down the road," he said.

"They were already actually working on very thin margins. All of a sudden they're actually out for three, four, five days or whatever it takes for them to recover. That could be the final straw."

Paying staff to do nothing

Owner of small Queensland business Regal Shower Screens, Tracey Tucker, said the lost day of business would cost at least $30,000, but there were numerous flow-on effects.

"I'm paying my girls sitting in here in the office to do nothing," she said.

"The phone rings, they can't order anything.

"Then it puts undue pressure because if it's back online on Monday, everything we missed Friday, we're going to try to catch up on."

Experts say the outage will hurt small business the most. (Reuters: Dado Ruvic/Illustration)

She said the outage meant the business would struggle to meet its promoted deadlines because the glass manufacturers would also be inundated on Monday.

"It's going to put pressure on everybody down the track because our girls are going to get yelled at, like, 'You just said my shower's going to be two weeks now, it's two and a half weeks', all because we can't send the order through today."

Challenges for IT staff

Service delivery manager with telecommunication company Hubify, Chloe Mombeshora, said she had received numerous calls from less tech-savvy clients who were unsure what was happening.

"They're thinking that their internet is down, they don't know what to do," she said.

She added some clients had raised concerns the inability to communicate could impact their businesses' reputations.

Some Outlook users were receiving notifications for emails they could not open. (ABC News: Liana Walker)

IT support specialist James Coates said he had been inundated with requests for help but was unable to reply through his helpdesk because it used Outlook.

"We actually have to call each client individually, every single personal phone number, every single Teams number, hope it gets through and update them that way because the email service is just not working on their end either," he said.

He said he also could not do other work over concerns it would not be saved.

Do you know more, or are you affected? If you're a business owner, essential worker, or have severely been impacted by this outage, share your story with us here.

Firms to reconsider Microsoft products

Liam Jones from the Australian Chamber of Commerce & Industry said the outage would have some businesses reconsidering using Microsoft.

"Businesses are constantly assessing which providers are going to give them the security and the reliability that they need. So I'm sure that there will be businesses out there looking at this," he said.

"This is a reminder of just the increasingly digital nature of the modern economy and disruptions like this can occur.

"They need to be worked through. We need to get to the bottom of what's occurred here and work out steps to ensure that disruptions like this don't occur into the future where they can be avoided."

He warned there would be ripple effects.

"But this is the digital world. This is the digital economy in which we live," he said.

Innes Willox says time is money. (ABC News: Dan Fermer)

Australian Industry Group chief executive Innes Willox said the outage demonstrated how important technology was to the modern economy, especially on a Friday when many hybrid workers would work from home.

"What the outage tells us is that technology is great until it isn't," he said.

" It's a reminder that businesses need to have backup plans in place, contingency plans for outages. "

He said the biggest issues would be communication and delays.

"Time is money and that disruption will be very difficult for some businesses, more difficult for some than others because it will represent lost opportunities," he said.

"So it's too early to even contemplate the impact, but this has global ramifications so it will lead to a significant downturn in productivity as well. And that will be of concern at a time when we need to drive productivity as much as possible."

title: Outback cattle flown to Kazakhstan
text:
Nearly 300 head of cattle from a station near Alice Springs have been flown to Kazakhstan, in what local producers hope is the start of a new market.

The distance from Alice Springs in the middle of Australia to Kazakhstan is roughly 10,000 kilometres.

Ben Hayes from Undoolya Station said he got a call from his livestock agent one day with an interesting offer.

"He asked if we had some heifers for this Kazakhstan job and we did," he said.

"The buyer from Kazakhstan actually flew out here [with an interpreter], took a quick look and ended up taking them.

"They got trucked down to Melbourne, where they stayed in quarantine for about a month and were then loaded into crates and onto the plane."

Cattle from Undoolya Station ready for export to Kazakhstan. (Supplied: Undoolya Station)

Mr Hayes said the animals were flown from Melbourne to Singapore and then onto Kazakhstan.

" I understand Kazakhstan's government have an initiative to boost their cattle breeding numbers, so they've taken some of our Herefords and will hopefully take some more next year. "

"There was a weight limit on them of about 180 to 250 kilograms and they had to be preg-tested empty."

He said the money paid for the animals was "on-par" with what he would normally receive in the Australian market.

But he said the chance to be involved in the sale to Kazakhstan was "very special".

"To know that our heifers are now becoming breeding stock for Kazakhstan is a feather in our cap, in Australia's cap," he said.

" Our cattle are off to Kazakhstan to help their industry and their breeding numbers. "

ABC Landline has been told some cattle from Mt Riddock Station in the NT were also purchased for the consignment.

According to data from the Federal Department of Agriculture, there were two flights of breeder cattle out of Victoria last month totalling 1,252 head.

Another flight to Kazakhstan took 1,617 breeder sheep.

It is understood Australia last exported cattle to Kazakhstan in 2019.

It is a long way from Alice Springs to Kazakhstan. (ABC Landline)

History of Undoolya exports

This is not the first time Undoolya Station has flown cattle to a distant market.

In 1981, Undoolya steers were flown direct out of Alice Springs to Korea.

"I was only a little fella at the time, but my father and grandfather flew steers out of Alice Springs on a Flying Tiger aircraft, straight to Korea" Mr Hayes said.

"I don't know why they wanted steers, but that's what happened, Alice Springs is an international airport, it was a good opportunity."

Undoolya Station is the Northern Territory's oldest pastoral lease. Established in 1872, the property has been owned by the Hayes family since 1906.

Watch ABC TV's Landline at 12:30pm on Sunday or on ABC iview.

title: The Rugby League World Cup final should have solved the Golden Boot battle
text:
The Golden Boot hasn't gone to the best player in the world for many years now but if it did you can still make the case it should have ended up in Reece Walsh's hands.

The Australian fullback is not always the best, but when he is at his best there's nobody better and his performances for the Kangaroos has been a scorching reminder that nobody in rugby league is as made for the fast lane.

These days the Golden Boot goes to the best player in Test matches for the year and by giving it to Kalyn Ponga after just 150 minutes in international football, the credibility of the award is on the line in Sunday's World Cup final.

World Cup opener a reminder of Australia's glory days There was a time when Test matches were rugby league's biggest, best and bloodiest spectacles, and last night's World Cup opener between Australia and New Zealand was a reminder of those days.

If New Zealand wins and Ponga plays well, two things that feel inextricably linked, it retroactively becomes a better decision. The outcome will be correct even if the process was flawed.

If Australia wins and Walsh plays well, it highlights the farce of giving out an accolade for international player of the year before the biggest international game of the year.

In a perfect world, or even an imperfect one given it just makes sense, the Golden Boot wouldn't be awarded until after full-time on Sunday, by which time Ponga could be a worthy winner, but as it stands Walsh should have won the trophy.

He has as many man-of-the-match awards in this tournament than Ponga has completed games and after a premiership hangover with Brisbane that could have killed a brown dog, the Australian jersey has banished the demons and brought Walsh roaring back to life.

Reece Walsh has been in brilliant form through the World Cup. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Sometimes he spins out of control, such as when he lost sight of a Samoa bomb in the semifinal, leading to a Stephen Crichton try, but when he stays on the road it's an exhilarating sight.

From his length-of-the-field try in the tournament opener against New Zealand to his five try assists against Cook Islands and a hat-trick against Samoa, Walsh's football over the past month has been reminiscent of the form he showed in leading Brisbane to the 2025 premiership.

It has served as a reminder of his game-bending abilities for anyone who needed it after a title defence to forget, and it's all the more impressive given his initial selection in this squad was far from guaranteed.

The loyalty of coach Kevin Walters played a major part and if James Tedesco had not played in the grand final, there's every chance he would have started against New Zealand in the tournament opener.

But right from the beginning, where Walsh won a brilliant duel with Ponga, he has made the spot his own and shaped Australia's fortunes along the way.

Ponga's win on awards night is just the prelude, with both men shaping as their country's best and most important players in Sunday's World Cup final.

It caps a year that has pulled back and forth between two of the biggest names and best players in the sport, and this last battle will determine who wins the war.

Ponga got the early running when he beat Walsh to the Queensland fullback job only for Walsh to strike back in their showdown three weeks ago that left both of them with stuffed highlight reels and Ponga with a broken arm.

The return from that injury has no doubt played a part in Ponga winning the award and while it's too early to be handing out Golden Boots there is no denying that his 150 minutes on the field for New Zealand has been exemplary.

Tedesco and Ponga walk different paths to grand final On Sunday, opposing fullbacks James Tedesco and Kalyn Ponga will lead their teams into the NRL grand final. It's about the only thing their paths have had in common.

Ponga linking up with the Kiwis wasn't possible until the Test eligibility laws were changed earlier this year, and what he's done since fits in with the wider journey he's been on this season.

It mirrors his run to the grand final with Newcastle, where he changed from being someone who could play great into a great player and it was a transformation based on emotion more-so than any technical improvement.

That evolution has continued through the World Cup, where he has proven the black and white jersey calls to him in a way the green and gold never did or could.

When the chance to represent Australia came up in the past he opted to stay home and prepare for the next NRL season.

When finally offered a shot for New Zealand not only did he accept, he rushed back from a serious injury and threw himself in front of Tongan freight trains without fear.

That feeling has unlocked something inside Ponga, which comes out as the most whole-hearted and inspiring play of his career.

He becomes what he was always said to be when he fully committed to a cause greater than himself.

That was not always possible in Newcastle, where Ponga's star power once overpowered the entire club, but it was this year and the same has been true for New Zealand throughout this tournament even as the new guy doubles as the most famous face on the team.

Where once he was cool and impenetrable to the point of being unknowable, now Ponga is throwing himself into contests heart first which is what makes his contrast with Walsh so compelling.

The Queensland teammates will fight it out for the right to be world champion. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The Bronco is all bleeding edges, all the time. What Ponga has learned to do is something Walsh does by compulsion. He could not hide his emotions if he tried and he never tries.

They come bursting out of him, as chest-beating when he rounded Ponga over the sideline against New Zealand or as acrobatics when he scored against Samoa.

He is desperate to excel, to strike fast and hard and deadly and most of all to win and sometimes Walsh wants it too much and chases it too hard, but it's one of those things you'd rather have too much of than not enough.

There will be a galaxy of stars fighting it out for the World Cup in Brisbane on Sunday, where the end of so many stories will be told.

Casey McLean, another Golden Boot nominee, is off to the fastest start for world domination since Alexander the Great and Jamayne Isaako is kicking goals from the middle of hurricanes.

Half of Isaah Yeo's chest is ripped apart and he's made 109 tackles while only missing two all tournament and he'll have to pull off a similar job if Australia is to slow New Zealand's astonishing forward pack.

Australia's old power conquers the new world Rugby league's Davids have gotten much bigger in recent times but Australia's win over Samoa in the World Cup semi-final was a reminder of Goliath's power.

Jahrome Hughes and Cameron Munster, whose playmaking genius is so often paired together with Melbourne, will fix both of their minds on the destruction of the other.

But nobody will have a greater impact on the winning and losing of it than Ponga and Walsh, two players who are so different yet have arrived in the same place as they both burn white hot.

If their meeting in Sydney was high noon, the sequel at Lang Park may as well be a one-horse town that ain't big enough for the both of them.

After they meet with guns drawn and the dust finally settles it'll prove a Golden Boot is one thing but being able to call yourself a world champion is quite another.

title: Historic lodge destroyed in blaze reopens after seven-year rebuild
text:
Perched high in the Gold Coast hinterland, surrounded by ancient rainforest, Binna Burra Lodge has captivated generations of visitors.

But in September 2019, that all came crashing down when devastating bushfires ripped through Lamington National Park.

The blaze devoured 6,000 hectares of rainforest, reducing the heritage-listed site, as well as 11 homes, to ashes.

Before: The lodge before the fire . . After: The lodge after the fire . . Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition Before and after images SLIDE The lodge before the fire / The lodge after the fire

But after enduring years of setbacks, including a pandemic and a cyclone, the treasured landmark has finally reopened to overnight guests.

"Recovery from disaster is not a short term process," Binna Burra Lodge chairman Steve Noakes said.

"In our case, it's been seven years, and it's just fantastic today to be welcoming people back to Binna Burra Lodge.

"Binna Burra's a place of a lot of intergenerational connection for the last almost 100 years and we hope that with this new lodge there'll be a whole lot of new generational connections."

Steve Noakes says the lodge is a treasured landmark. (Supplied: Binna Burra Lodge)

Lodge fills generations with 'awe'

Binna Burra Lodge was founded by conservationists Arthur Groom and Romeo Lahey in the 1930s.

The two men wanted to create a place where people could soak up the region's lush natural beauty, while being inspired to protect the rainforests into the future.

Arthur Groom and Romeo Lahey founded Binna Burra Lodge. (Supplied: Binna Burra Lodge)

"Over generations, lots and lots of people from around Australia and around the world have had the opportunity to experience the location," Mr Noakes said.

" All of them have been filled with awe. "

The bushfire tore through Lamington National Park. (ABC News: Jennifer Huxley)

But on September 8, 2019, a blaze tore through the area, leaving a trail of destruction in its wake.

Evacuated three days before, Mr Noakes still remembers the moment he discovered the lodge was gone.

"[An] ABC report was the first time we had confirmation the lodge had been destroyed," he said.

Before: The lodge dinner bell before the fire . . After: The lodge dinner bell after the fire . . Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition Before and after images SLIDE The lodge dinner bell before the fire / The lodge dinner bell after the fire

Report casts doubt over cause of blaze

Police initially reported the blaze may have been sparked by a discarded cigarette.

But an internal Queensland Fire and Emergency Services report, obtained by the ABC, found the fire was more likely started at a mystery shooting range in bushland.

The fire burnt through 6,000 hectares of rainforest. (Supplied: Binna Burra Lodge)

The report also contained evidence claiming that, during the fire, firefighters left one containment point, logging it as being "under control" when it was not.

The blaze then raged out of control, consuming the lodge and surrounding homes.

Several homes were lost in the bushfires. (AAP: Glenn Hunt)

Mr Noakes said while the reopening had been "a long time coming", there was "never a question" the lodge would be rebuilt.

"I wasn't sure how we were going to do it," he said.

" It's taken seven years, but we're across the finish line. "

The new lodge has been designed to protect against future disasters. (ABC Gold Coast)

New building specially designed

Mr Noakes said the new facility was designed with concrete structures wrapped in timber facades to ensure better protection against future disasters.

"It's very different from the old lodge which was beautiful old heritage timber, but of course when bushfire comes through it just all gets sizzled up," he said.

"If the worst thing ever happened and a fire did finally get through, the basic infrastructure would still be there to enable repair."

The rebuild has taken seven years. (ABC Gold Coast)

Gold Coast architect and bushfire-mitigation expert Eldon Bottcher said while building design was crucial, it was only one piece of the puzzle to prevent future disasters.

"We've got to look at how we manage our vegetation around the building," he said.

"We need to make sure we can get firefighters in around the place and we need to make sure we've got a dedicated water supply for those firefighters.

"There's a whole pile of things we've got to do."

title: Cummins hopes his answers ended the sandpaper war. He is sadly mistaken
text:
If nothing else, nobody can ever say that Pat Cummins didn't front up and face the music.

For 70 minutes he stood there, smiling through whatever other emotion was boiling inside of him, disarming with charm and eloquence and just enough humour for the situation at hand. He took the questions until they dried up.

He lifted the lid on cricket's uncomfortable history with ball tampering, detailing specific examples he had seen within Test and Sheffield Shield cricket. He said he believed Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were punished much too harshly by Cricket Australia.

Cummins hits out at Khawaja Australian Test cricket captain Pat Cummins rubbishes Usman Khawaja's ball-tampering claims in a long and passionate press conference.

He spoke to the 2018 Australian team's "ugly underbelly", addressed allegations of systemic racism within the sport, and spoke about the culture of casual verbal abuse that stretched all the way to suburban club cricket.

Cummins provided a detailed floor plan of the Newlands dressing rooms, and mustered a laugh despite his obvious distaste for the cameras which captured he and his wife conversing on the street.

He pledged to be as open as possible, to dig into the game's nuances — he used that word a lot — to explain as much of what happened in that Cape Town Test match as he could.

And his verdict, repeated multiple times and with precise wording, was clear: Pat Cummins did not know sandpaper was being used to tamper with the ball, and Usman Khawaja's version of events is incorrect.

Pat Cummins rejected allegations made by Usman Khawaja in his book Sabr. (ABC News)

Was he telling the truth? Who really knows. David Warner says he wasn't.

The technicality Cummins and his fellow bowlers have relied upon since they released their first statement of denial in 2021 was that they did not know "sandpaper had been brought out onto the field". Those words have been repeated often this week, presented carefully each time.

By Khawaja's version of events, as printed in his book Sabr, that leaves some wriggle room in which perhaps there was wider knowledge sandpaper was being used on the sidelines in breaks of play when the umpire had left the ball on the boundary.

Sandpaper response plagued by error Usman Khawaja's revelations on Sandpapergate may have come eight years after the fact, but time has not changed Australia's response to the cricket scandal.

But Cummins was questioned about that too, and once again had a firm and unflinching answer.

"That was news to me this week. I had no idea," Cummins said.

"Even chatting to a couple of the guys, that was a revelation to ourselves. That was one of the things that really surprised us because that doesn't happen anymore; the umpires give the ball to you out in the middle."

The good news is that is a fact someone will be able to check.

Somewhere in the SuperSport archives there will surely be footage of the players coming onto the ground after the breaks in play during that series, and surely in that it will be clear to see precisely when the ball is exchanged between umpire and players.

The bad news is that is just about the only fact that can be checked. Everything else is hearsay, one man's word against another, a civil war whose weapons are alternate offerings of "my truth" and "my story".

Cummins suggested the past eight years have weighed on Khawaja, and hinted that may be because, as Khawaja expressed in his book, he specifically knew about the plan to bring sandpaper onto the field and even warned Cameron Bancroft to be careful.

What does Khawaja think about that pretty loaded suggestion? We will surely find out soon enough, either on Instagram or on the next stop on the book tour.

David Warner says Pat Cummins threw Usman Khawaja under the bus. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

We already know what Warner thinks. He said he believed Cummins threw Khawaja under the bus.

This just days after Khawaja had to deny he had thrown Cummins and co under the bus. At this point, there is not a member of the Australian cricket team who does not reside beneath a bus.

Warner said on Fox Cricket he would not be able to move on until the truth came out. The truth, he says, is what is written in Khawaja's book.

Warner was given the opportunity to expound on that truth in his own words, but did not take it, suggesting instead a future book of his own would eventually do that job.

It's all a total mess. Social media reaction to Cummins's conference suggests the Australian public, growing increasingly fatigued by it all, has long since made up its mind on what really went on in Cape Town and is past the point of being swayed by new information.

At some point, most likely when all of these players are comfortable in retirement and these squabbles make up part of the nostalgia tour rather than dominate the discourse, we may wonder what all the fuss was about.

The biggest error of the Cummins Q and A was his belief that his appearance would allow everyone to draw a line under the affair and move on.

That's not happening. We're dealing with hurt feelings here, fractured relationships and bruised egos and nebulous concepts of truth and justice. You better pick your side, if you haven't already, because this is never going away.

title: David Warner slams Pat Cummins over Sandpapergate denial
text:
Former Australia opener David Warner has stood by Usman Khawaja's revelations about the 2018 Sandpapergate scandal, saying Australia captain Pat Cummins threw Khawaja "under the bus" at a press conference in Sydney this morning.

Cummins had said Khawaja's claims that the entire Australian camp knew about ball tampering in Cape Town were "complete and utter nonsense", repeating that he had no prior knowledge of plans for using sandpaper to illegally alter the ball.

Warner, who was vice captain at the time of the incident and who received a year-long ban for his involvement, said he was "very disappointed" by his former captain on Fox Cricket's coverage of the opening ODI between Australia and England in Perth.

"I feel the captain today threw Ussie under the bus and I'm very, very disappointed by that," Warner said.

Warner said Cummins threw Khawaja "under the bus" at this morning's press conference. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett/Cricket Australia)

Warner also stood by his assertion that the initial investigation had been "botched", and that he, along with fellow suspended players Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft, had no choice but to bear the blame.

"The way it was handled in the first place, it was hard for us to go back and give more evidence. I feel like it was a botched investigation," Warner said.

"It was a quick one to get it over and done with. Some of the questions were quite challenging in the way it was being planted on us and we had to move on and just accept responsibility, the three of us, and we ultimately did.

"We don't have that opportunity to go there and speak again. [Cricket Australia CEO] Todd Greenberg squashed that the other day. There probably are going to be conversations behind the scenes after this."

Cummins hits out at Khawaja Australian Test cricket captain Pat Cummins rubbishes Usman Khawaja's ball-tampering claims in a long and passionate press conference.

Warner, a childhood friend of Khawaja's, also said he expected the truth about the saga to come out eventually.

"It's inevitable. Everyone writes a book at the end of their career but for me it's about accepting the truth and I just don't think this will rest," Warner said.

"It's very, very difficult with the acceptance of the consequences that we live day to day in our lives."

Warner described the blame levelled at him, Smith and Bancroft a "life punishment", saying he and wife Candice experienced a miscarriage in the aftermath of the incident.

"All three of us have paid a big price in this and I hadn't spoken about it in eight years, but at the end of the day, we've got to live with these consequences daily," Warner said.

"And we've been served a life punishment. So when other people talk about that they've been affected by it, there's nothing worse than for me, Steve and Cameron, who have to walk over there every single day and we cop abuse.

"Yes, we accepted it, but at the end of the day, my wife and I as well pay the greatest price.

"We lost a baby during that time. And that's why it really hurts me the most until the truth is accepted."

Earlier today, Cummins claimed he could not explain why Khawaja's and Warner's recollections of the incident were so different to his.

"That sounds like a pretty good question for those two," Cummins said.

"Again, there's quite a few different accounts here, so they've got two accounts.

"There's 11 players in that room, so that means there's nine other guys who I think it's appropriate you give an equal amount of weight into their story as well."

title: Mount Isa's $145 million critical minerals pitch one step closer
text:
Mount Isa's push to reinvent its regional economy with a new mineral research hub has secured state and federal backing for a feasibility study.

Mount Isa City Council and the University of Queensland released a business case earlier this month for a $145 million critical minerals research centre.

The facility would allow mining companies to analyse rock samples from local mineral deposits to see what minerals were present and if they would be viable to mine.

The $145 million centre is expected to create up to 50 permanent jobs. (Supplied: Mount Isa City Council)

In July 2025, Mount Isa's underground copper mine closure saw nearly 500 workers sacked in the 19,000-strong community, forcing the council to search for economic alternatives.

While Mount Isa's economy has been affected, exploration and investment across the wider North West Minerals Province has boomed, with about 85 critical minerals projects underway.

Sustainable Minerals Institute director at the University of Queensland Rick Valenta said the proposed hub would allow industry to scale operations quickly.

Rick Valenta (right) says the facility will help mines understand what minerals are in deposits and how they could be mined. (ABC Rural: Eric Barker)

"The reason you can't just find a deposit and put it into production in a year is because you've got to answer … 'What's the content of the metal that you're after? And … how do we get the metals out of that rock?'" Professor Valenta said.

"[At the moment], those rocks would be going elsewhere in Queensland … Australia or the world … [and] that involves a cost and a delay.

"This centre is aimed at providing a local solution to that sort of thing."

The proposed research centre would be situated between the George Fisher Mine and Mount Isa Airport. (Supplied: Mount Isa City Councill)

Search for new ideas

Mount Isa Mayor Peta MacRae said she hoped the research hub would help future-proof the city by giving mining companies a dedicated site to research problems locally.

"[Currently] minerals are just going to be ripped up and shipped," she said.

"What we want to do is add the value and do as much processing as we can … to help us secure the future for our communities."

Peta MacRae hopes the project will centralise some of the regions' mining investment into the town's economy. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

The proposed hub is expected to create up to 50 permanent jobs and would be located near the Mount Isa Airport.

On Friday morning, Federal Assistant Minister for Resources Anthony Chisholm confirmed funding would be released to consider the proposal.

"We want to make the most of these opportunities … and ensure that Mount Isa remains a great place to live and work and attract people at the same time," he said.

"We know that there is enormous potential, but it's about proving that and then also ensuring that we can attract the industry investment."

Anthony Chisholm says the cenrre is about proving Mt Isa's potential and attracting industry investment. (ABC News: Tim Little)

The federal and state governments have agreed to tip in $241,250 each to fund a feasibility study, with an additional $482,500 to come from Mount Isa City Council.

If successful, the hub would operate in conjunction with similar facilities in Mackay and Townsville.

Initial testing and analysis would start at Mount Isa's centre, before small-scale piloting took place in Mackay followed by large-scale trials in Townsville.

title: Vandals increasingly targeting Melbourne's bus shelters, data suggests
text:
Reports of vandalism across Victoria's public transport network have increased by 50 per cent over the past year according to a popular app.

The creator of Snap Send Solve claims it received more than 5,700 reports of vandalism and graffiti on public transport across Victoria between October 2025 and last month.

That was up from 3,760 the year prior.

Bus shelters were the most common target for vandals, with nearly 3,700 reports received in the past 12 months — double those of bus shelter vandalism reports from the previous year.

Bus shelters are commonly damaged in Victoria. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

"This isn't a general rise in vandalism, and it isn't app growth," said Snap Send Solve chief executive Danny Gorog, whose app launched in 2013.

Vandals were targeting "shelters specifically", he said.

Where in Melbourne is worst affected by bus shelter vandalism?

Snap Send Solve's bus shelter figures include all reports of vandalism or graffiti to the app in Victoria which describe bus shelters or stops.

Mr Gorog said they received about two million reports annually for issues ranging from potholes to graffiti, from some 1.25 million registered users across Australia and New Zealand.

In Melbourne, suburbs in the north-east and south-east recorded the highest number of bus shelter vandalism reports.

Graffiti and broken glass were the issues most frequently flagged by users.

The Victorian government confirmed bus shelter vandalism was the most common type of vandalism across the state's public transport network, but did not provide a figure for the repair cost.

It said about $10 million was spent each year removing and repairing graffiti on the train network.

Public Transport Users Association spokesperson Daniel Bowen said bus shelter vandalism was a particular nuisance, especially during hot and wet weather extremes.

"Anecdotally, there are too many cases of vandalism," Mr Bowen said.

" We all want a reliable public transport system, one that is pleasant to use and [where] every seat is available for passengers. "

Bus shelters are often spray-painted or scratched by vandals. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

While bus shelter vandalism accounted for fewer than half of all public transport vandalism reports Snap Send Solve received in 2024-25, it was nearly two-thirds of reports in 2025-26.

"There's clearly a problem there," Mr Gorog said.

Responsibility for repairing or removing bus shelter vandalism across Melbourne varies between location.

Shelters with electronic billboards are often the responsibility of the advertising company leasing them.

Vandalism destroys Melbourne cricket pitch A local cricket club in the south-western suburbs has expressed dismay after its turf pitch was destroyed by suspected vandals on e-bikes.

The ABC contacted several local governments within the areas with the highest number of bus shelter vandalism reports made to Snap Send Solve.

Most declined to comment and deferred to the Department of Transport and Planning, or to oOh!media, which leases shelters for advertising.

Mr Gorog said one theory was that lingering damage, such as graffiti not immediately removed, could encourage further vandalism.

"There is a thesis that there's this repair lag ... and when something has deteriorated and has been vandalised, it creates a bit more vandalism," Mr Gorog said.

Drones, CCTV used in monitoring

The Shire of Nillumbik, which contains suburbs including Eltham and Diamond Creek, is in the north-east of Melbourne where the highest number of shelter vandalism reports originated.

The Shire said it had received 130 vandalism reports since January — roughly one every two days.

It said shelters were inspected and cleaned twice weekly, "with graffiti removed as quickly as possible".

Officials at Frankston City, in Melbourne's south-east, said they had removed more than 37,000 square metres of graffiti across all property types last financial year.

The council has been running a trial offering locals $500 if their graffiti reports result in a guilty finding in court.

Another scheme offered offered free graffiti removal supplies to locals.

Public Transport Users Association spokesperson Daniel Bowen said "there are too many cases of vandalism" on Victoria's bus network. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

The Department of Transport and Planning said it used more than 14,000 CCTV cameras across the public transport network.

A spokesperson said the department was "cracking down" on vandalism using drones and "new tracking technology" along train routes.

“We encourage anyone who sees vandalism or damaged property on our network to report it to Victoria Police," the spokesperson said.

title: Victorian Labor MP 'sick to death' of council approach to new Maryborough pool
text:
Labor's Ripon MP Martha Haylett has called on Central Goldfields Shire Council Mayor Ben Green and CEO Peter Harriott to "reconsider their positions" amid controversy surrounding the redevelopment of Maryborough outdoor swimming pool.

The pool has been closed since 2022 after an independent assessor deemed it was at "end of life".

The Labor MP announced yesterday if re-elected, the government would match a Liberal Party promise of a further $5 million to fund the Central Victorian pool under "very strict conditions".

"We will not release a single cent of taxpayer funding until the council is able to explain how they have so dramatically mismanaged this project, and provide the community with a fully transparent and detailed plan as to how they intend to actually deliver it," Ms Haylett said.

"We are sick to death of this council repeatedly coming and asking for further money.

Martha Haylett has accused the council of mismanaging the Maryborough outdoor pool project. (Supplied)

"Due to ongoing issues, we think it is appropriate that Liberal Mayor Ben Green and CEO Peter Harriott reconsider their positions."

Yesterday, Liberal Party candidate Megan Read pledged $5 million to demolish the existing pool and build a new 50-metre outdoor pool.

$9 million in funding has already been secured for the project, comprising $4.5 million federal commitment, $3 million from the state government and $1.5 million from the Central Goldfields Shire Council.

Nationals candidate Jo Armstrong has also promised to "deliver the pool to the community".

Ben Green is the Central Goldfields Shire mayor. (Supplied)

An assessor previously recommended the Maryborough pool be demolished and rebuilt, estimated to cost $9 million.

Last year, the estimated cost of reopening the pool jumped to about $14 million, which the council attributed to soaring construction prices and site complexities.

The 50-metre pool is the only outdoor facility of its kind for the town of 8,000 residents.

Maryborough is facing its fourth summer without an outdoor pool. (ABC News: Sarah Lawrence)

Central Goldfields Shire Council did not respond to the ABC's questions about the call for the mayor or CEO to resign or to allegations the council had "dramatically mismanaged" the pool project.

In a statement to the ABC, a Central Goldfields Shire Council spokesperson welcomed the Coalition and Labor's commitment to provide $5 million for the pool.

"Additional community engagement will occur around all aspects of the project when funding is secured," the spokesperson said.

"After the election outcome is known, we'll seek the local member's support to work collaboratively and get on with delivering."

Speaking to the ABC this morning, CEO Peter Harriott said the $5 million commitment was "fantastic", but he denied wrongdoing.

"There has been no mismanagement of this project. If you are talking about the costs … look at some of the tunnels in Melbourne that go [over the budget]. We are nowhere in the league of those increases," Mr Harriott said.

title: 'That's on you': Queanbeyan council defends caravan parking policy
text:
The Queanbeyan-Palerang Regional Council has begun enforcing strict residential parking rules banning large caravans, boats, and trailers from long-term parking in residential streets.

The push is part of the council's effort to crackdown on large vehicles being left for long periods of time in prime parking spots.

Under the new rules, which came into effect last month, vehicles longer than 7.5 metres cannot park in residential streets for more than an hour.

Vehicles smaller than 7.5 metres will be allowed to park in residential streets for up to 28 days before being required to move.

The council's push is aimed at reclaiming street space, and is being met with mixed reactions. (ABC News: Ruby Thomas)

Queanbeyan-Palerang Regional Council Mayor Kenrick Winchester said the issue was prominent in the NSW town of Googong, where he said people were using on-street parking to store large vehicles.

The mayor said people had "bought houses where they can't fit their boat or their trailer in their own backyards, or sheds, or driveways, and so they're parking them randomly throughout the suburb".

"You bought a house out at Googong and you didn't plan to fit your big boat or caravan on the property that you bought, then that's all on you I guess," he said.

The new council rules also ban any vehicles from parking on the verge — the area between the road and the boundary of a property.

The council's pursuit to reclaim street space has been met with mixed reactions.

The council is concerned that vehicles are being left for long periods of time in prime parking spots. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

'A good thing': home owners

Local couple, Sarah and Parveen, have lived in Googong for nine years and said they had recently seen more caravans parked on their street, for months at a time.

The couple said they now referred to their street as a "caravan park".

Googong residents Sarah and Parveen welcome the enforcement of strict residential parking rules, targeting caravans, boats, and trailers. (ABC News)

"In the beginning it was not bad, but now this whole street sometimes is full of caravans," Sarah said.

"Most of the year they just stay there, except the few times people will take them for holidays."

Parveen said the vehicles, which he speculated were not always owned by people who lived on the street, created a safety hazard.

"This street … has a bend in it and caravans are a bit wider, they take [up the] whole lane. It's hard to see over the bend ... so I think [the decision] is a good thing," Parveen said.

'Drive around the corner, don't be afraid to exercise'

But the move has also resulted in some not-so-happy campers.

The Campervan and Motorhome Club of Australia (CMCA) has criticised the crackdown as heavy-handed and unnecessary.

Chief executive Richard Barwick said people would now have to pay for storage sites for the vehicles, on top of rising fuel costs.

Vehicles longer than 7.5 metres can no longer park in residential streets for more than an hour. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

"Don't pick a certain market because they think it's an easy target and that they are wealthy because not all people that own an RV or that own a boat are wealthy people," he said.

" We have a lot of pensioners in our organisation that are struggling with the cost of living and this extra burden will affect [them]. "

Mr Barwick said he also did not believe that the area had the population or density to warrant the new rules, saying there was likely plenty of parking available for local residents.

"I know Queanbeyan reasonably well; to me there'd be parking. Drive around the corner, don't be afraid to exercise."

title: The superchip genius or the big name wildcard? Eight contenders to replace Huang as Nvidia’s CEO

Eight contenders to replace Huang as Nvidia’s CEO Wyatte Grantham-Philips Updated November 13, 2026 — 5:09pm ,first published 3:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Nvidia chief Jensen Huang has resigned from his top post at the chipmaker he co-founded, after reports of the tech titan’s extramarital affairs came into the spotlight this week. One of those relationships has raised national security concerns. The New York Times reported that Huang had an affair with a businesswoman US intelligence suspects to be a Chinese spy, which Beijing denies. Separately, the outlet and later others found Huang was said to have had another affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him directly – compounding calls for him to step down. Reports of a third affair, this time with another Nvidia employee, emerged on Friday following his resignation. Jensen Huang turned Nvidia into one of the biggest companies in the world before a dramatic fall from grace. Bloomberg Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation, effective immediately. The California-based company said that Colette Kress – who has been Nvidia’s chief financial officer and executive vice president since 2013 – will step into the role of interim chief executive. The scandal marks the most tumultuous chapter yet for Nvidia, whose high-end chips have emerged as the leading building blocks for artificial intelligence. Huang has become a key face in the AI race, both across the industry and often on US President Donald Trump’s side in Washington.

Advertisement

Here’s what we know. Who is Nvidia’s interim chief executive? Nvidia says that Colette Kress is now interim chief executive. Before joining Nvidia more than 13 years ago, Kress worked at Cisco, Microsoft and Texas Instruments in various roles, according to her executive biography on the company’s website. Colette Kress has been named as Nvidia’s interim chief executive. In a statement about her new post on Thursday, Kress said that Nvidia’s “strength has always come from its people” and that she was “committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years”.

Advertisement

The company’s board of directors also said that it had named its first-ever chairman, Harvey C. Jones, an entrepreneur and venture investor. Who is Alice Huang? Over the weekend, following news reports of Huang’s relationship with a woman identified as former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, Nvidia’s then chief executive apologised for being “unfaithful to my wife”. Jensen Huang and Alice Huang pictured at a Shanghai restaurant. “My actions hurt her and our children,” Huang wrote in an email to employees, adding that his colleagues also “deserve better” from him.

Advertisement

Neither Huang nor Nvidia identified who he had been intimate with by name, but the apology arrived shortly after Nvidia said it was investigating whether Huang had been “the target of a foreign intelligence effort”. Last month, the Times reported that US intelligence agencies discovered Nvidia’s Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang, who also goes by the name Huang Le – and determined she was feeding information directly to Beijing. (Huang is a common surname and the two are not related.) Who is Kimberly Powell? The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare. The Times reported Huang, 63, and Powell, 48, were captured on video being affectionate at a San Jose, California, hotel during an Nvidia conference in March. Both Huang and Powell are married to other people.

Advertisement

The New York Times reported Huang had engaged in a second affair with one of his subordinates, Kimberly Powell, who is Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare. Nvidia’s code of conduct instructs staff to avoid situations that could create conflict, including “personal relationships”. Who is Lori Huang? The scandal also has ramifications for Huang’s personal life. Huang’s admission has fuelled speculation about the fate of his 41-year marriage with Lori Huang, 64. She is president of the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation, which had $US9 billion ($13.1 billion) in assets as of 2024, including $US6 billion in fresh funding that year. Of Jensen Huang’s 922 million Nvidia shares, more than half belong to a trust where he and Lori Huang are the co-trustees, according to financial filings. She is also the sole controller of a trust that owns about $US5 billion worth of Nvidia shares. Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, walk to the White House to attend a state dinner hosted for Chinese President Xi Jinping in September. AP Photo/Carolyn Kaster

Advertisement

Lori Huang joins a small group of tech titan spouses who have had to grapple with public infidelity. The list includes MacKenzie Scott, the ex-wife of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, and Melinda French Gates, ex-wife of Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates. The succession problem: who might replace Huang? Huang co-founded Nvidia back in 1993, and had led the company ever since, with no clear successor in sight. Huang’s ouster has led to a scramble for a new permanent chief executive, and Nvidia said it was considering both “internal and external candidates”. Donald Trump nominated former Apple chief Tim Cook as an ideal candidate to take over as Nvidia CEO. AP As well as Kress, various other names have been floated as potential successors, including Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky, Nvidia executive Ian Buck – credited as the tech genius behind the CUDA software that allows developers to write code on the company’s chips, AMD chief executive Lisa Su (who is a cousin of Jensen Huang), Arm boss Rene Haas, former Google chief Eric Schmidt and Intel chief executive Lip-Bu Tan. US President Donald Trump also weighed in, saying former Apple chief Tim Cook should take the role.

Advertisement

“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple,” Trump said on social media. “A Legend replaces a Legend!” he added. Where investigations stand Nvidia hasn’t provided any notable new updates in its internal review that was first announced at the weekend. At the time, the company said it had “no reason to believe” that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information. Trump was reportedly briefed about intelligence findings involving Huang well before the scandal erupted publicly. But when asked at the weekend whether he wished he had acted sooner on that information, the president said, “I don’t think so”, and maintained that Nvidia’s chief executive was an “honorable guy”. Loading

Advertisement

Trump later said the FBI was looking into Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, although where exactly that probe stands is unclear. Meanwhile, lawmakers from both sides of the aisle on Capitol Hill are calling for further investigations. Many eyes have been on Nvidia’s ties to Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which prominently touts the companies’ partnership on its website. Last year, Megaspeed was accused of illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China, but in December said there was “no evidence” of such exports. On Thursday, Megaspeed maintained that it took its obligation to comply with American export control laws “extremely seriously” – and that it was committed to working “constructively and transparently” with the US government. Singaporean authorities said they questioned Alice Huang and confiscated her passport last year as part of an investigation into Megaspeed. They concluded there wasn’t enough evidence that she had committed a crime, but suspected she provided “inaccurate information” to downplay her role at Megaspeed and barred her from returning to the country. China, meanwhile, has denied that it attempted to ensnare Jensen Huang. Its Foreign Ministry earlier this week called the spying allegations “unsubstantiated” and said they amount to a smear campaign.

Advertisement

What is it with the leather jackets? Jensen Huang has become known for his vast collection of leather jackets. They have become a staple of his wardrobe and his persona, and were his trademark look while delivering speeches. Huang credits wife Lori and daughter Madison with coming up with the look. He is reported to have 60 jackets in his wardrobe. A Tom Ford leather jacket worn and signed by Huang, sold in July at a Sotheby’s auction for $US960,000. The proceeds were donated to charity. Huang has become known for his leather jackets. AP Photo/John Locher

Advertisement

Donald and Jensen’s bromance Huang has maintained a close relationship to Trump throughout the Republican president’s second term in office. He has successfully lobbied for looser AI regulation overall – including less strict limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China. And he is among tech chief executives who have dined at the White House, and even travelled on Air Force One. Trump has called Huang “smart” and “amazing”, repeatedly insisting he join him on foreign trips. After news of his resignation broke on Thursday, the president maintained that Huang had done “done a fantastic job”. Huang and Donald Trump at the US Institute of Peace in Washington. AP

The entrepreneur praised Trump effusively in 2025 before a meeting. “I come with only one purpose only, which is to inform and to be in service of the president as he thinks about how to make America great,” Huang told reporters. Nvidia committed $US25 million to help fund Trump’s White House ballroom renovation, a major personal priority for the president in his second term. Last month, Trump presented Jensen Huang with the National Medal of Science. On Friday, Trump said Huang called him and expressed remorse over what the scandal had done to his family. Trump, in a White House interview with the broadcaster Stephen A. Smith on Thursday, praised Huang just hours after his ouster. “What he’s done is incredible,” Trump said. “Nvidia is unbelievable.

“I spoke to him yesterday. He’s going through hell. What he feels most badly about is his wife and family. That’s what he told me. He called me.” How has this affected Nvidia’s share price? Nvidia shares closed 4.3 per cent lower and have tumbled this week, wiping nearly $US500 billion off the market capitalisation of the company. The company is now valued around $US4 trillion, having been worth more than $US5.8 trillion in early October. Nvidia’s value has plummeted this week. Bloomberg Jensen Huang’s personal net worth has fallen by about $US19 billion this week, dropping him out of the world’s top 10 richest people list, according to Forbes. He is now the 13th richest person in the world with a net worth of about $US143 billion.

A new test for the AI industry The shockwaves of Huang’s exit stress just how few figures hold so much power in the AI race. Nvidia is one of the world’s most valuable companies today – and Huang has risen to fame across the tech world. Related Article Analysis

He may have broken one of them Some analysts suspect that the foreign intelligence allegations will strengthen calls in Washington for stricter export controls with China, which could in turn renew trade strains overall. Others have called it a watershed moment for Nvidia, the chipmaker that has long been seen as the crown jewel for powering AI. And questions of security risks facing the companies at the forefront of this technology are piling up Stephanie Balaouras, group research director for Forrester, said Huang’s resignation from Nvidia wasn’t just a test for the company but the AI boom as a whole.

As one of the most experienced members of female jockeys’ rooms in Sydney and its surrounds, Alysha Collett tries to help out the growing number of apprentices whenever she can. It is support the 32-year-old group 1-winner feels was missing in the far sparser rooms when she was coming through the ranks. Jockey Alysha Collett. Getty Images And it is support needed more than ever this week after the heartbreaking death of Scone apprentice Izzy Neale. “It’s a little family in that jockeys’ room, and it’s honestly just devastating,” said Collett, who rides $5.50 favourite Sweynesday in the $1 million The Hunter on Saturday at Newcastle.

“It’s really unfair what’s happened, but the girls have all stuck together, which is really nice to see. “Izzy was just a lovely girl. It’s heartbreaking. Izzy Neale in July. Getty Images “Mikayla [Weir] and Maddy [Owen] and others, they were good friends with her. I don’t know what they would be going through right now. It’s brutal, and it’s a bit of reality, for what things can happen, for the young apprentices as well. That’s probably the tough thing to swallow also.” Neale’s family announced the 22-year-old’s death on Tuesday night, following a fall at Warren on Sunday when her mount Marnoo broke down on the home turn with a catastrophic injury.

Advertisement

It was the first race fall death of a jockey in NSW since Darren Jones in 2017 and has triggered an outpouring of grief and tributes for Neale, who had been riding professionally for less than three years. The tragedy has rocked the racing community, especially the huge group of female apprentices in NSW. Collett rides regularly at all levels and often makes herself available as an adviser in stewards inquiries, or mentor outside of them, for her younger colleagues. Female apprentices (back) Mollie Fitzgerald, Siena Grima, Olivia Chambers, Izzy Neale, Coriah Keatings, Rebecca Bronett Prag, (front) Anna Roper and Shannen Llewellyn at Rosehill on June 27. Getty Images “I want them to do well because when I was younger I never really had that help, so if I can help them in any way possible, I try to do it,” Collett said. “If they ever ask what did I think of that ride, or what could I have done different, we are all open for opinions and help, all us seniors, like Rachel [King] as well. It’s nice we are able to do that.”

Collett heads to Newcastle’s annual standalone on Saturday with the main job of riding winners, and she has strong chances in the day’s richest two races. She has picked up the ride on Annabel and Rob Archibald-trained Sweynesday in the Hunter. The six-year-old came from last to finish a close second to Ndola in the GH Mumm Rising Fast Stakes (1200m) two weeks ago at Flemington in what was his second start since coming from the Roger James and Robert Wellwood stable. He has drawn well in gate six for the 16-strong 1300m quality and Collett hoped to capitalise. “It’s a really open market, but we’ve drawn a good barrier,” she said. “His run the other day was brilliant in Melbourne. “I’ve ridden it once early doors, but he seems pretty straightforward.

“From the bad barrier in nine the other day over 1200m, they were a little bit sharp, so they looked to ride him where he was happy, but from the better barrier we might try to utilise that. We’ll have to talk about that. “There’s a good amount of pace in the race, which is nice. There’s a bit of pressure, which I think will fall into his lap nicely.” Collett also rides Todd Pollard-trained Zuleika ($6.50) in the $300,000 Beauford (2300m). She was aboard when the mare was third to Anthracite at Randwick over 1600m, before she was eighth last Saturday in the Matriarch (2000m) at Flemington. “I rode her two starts back and she went brilliant,” she said. “I’m excited to get back on her, over a 2300 set up, too. To me, if there was another 200m in that Randwick run, she would have just kept picking up and going, so I thought for a mile run, it was super.

“She’s got great tactical speed and she’s a great horse to ride because she goes forward and when you ask her to come back, she comes back and relaxes.” Maher getting Fawkner Park on track Declan Maher would do well to one-up his big brother, Ciaron, given the run the champion trainer is on. Tempted’s Everest win and a history-making Melbourne Cup trifecta have led a remarkable spring for the Victorian. Declan, though, can claim bragging rights, of sorts, if he can get veteran stayer Fawkner Park to fire in the $300,000 Beauford (2300m) on Saturday at Newcastle.

Advertisement

Fawkner Park, now eight, raced at a high level for the Annabel and Rob Archibald stable, winning the $1.2 million Q22 and placing three times in group 1s, before going to Ciaron Maher. After one poor run and two trials, the trainer convinced connections to send Fawkner Park to his brother’s new Gold Coast stable, which he established in April last year. Declan Maher (right) with Ciaron Maher and jockey William McCarthy. Getty Images “Ciaron just wasn’t completely happy with him and since I’d moved to Queensland, he’d met Kurt Gasky, my physio, and he had worked on a few Ciaron had sent up here,” Declan said. “He just thought he needed that regular maintenance.”

Fawkner Park, a $10 chance in the Beauford, is unplaced in seven starts since the move, but Declan feels he can challenge on Saturday after finishing four and a half lengths away over 1815m last week at Eagle Farm. “When I got him, he ran really well first up in the winter and then he got a little splint,” he said. “It muddled up that preparation a bit, so we reset. “I thought he ran really well first up, then I elected to leave him in Sydney and it was probably the wrong call. He requires a bit of maintenance with his body. Kurt does a lot with him to keep him free and moving at his best, so I got him home after that and he ran really well last Saturday. “It was more like an 1800m trial. They went slow in front and ran home quick. For where he was, and the weight he had, it was a big ask, but he bounced through the run and has been really fresh all week and I’ve been really keen to get him out to that trip on Saturday.

Declan Maher. Vicky Hughson “He’s got a bit of an enigma about him, that’s why I’ve had a few gears changes on him. An old gelding, you’ve got to keep him thinking a bit. “But his last 600 the other day was one of his best in a dozen starts. If he let go like he can, he’s right in it.” Declan, who has a team of 20, worked closely with Ciaron for many years before going out on his own, but the brothers still help each other out. Fawkner Park travelled to Ciaron’s Bobs Farm property on Thursday. “I’m still working indirectly with my brother,” he said.

“It’s good, and it’s also handy if we need to chew the fat over a few things. He’s a handy bloke to have a conversation with.” He hopes to take Fawkner Park to the Christmas Cup at Randwick on December 12, if he runs well on Saturday.

Australian Gold and Copper has delivered a spectacular polymetallic intersection from its Evergreen project in NSW’s highly endowed South Cobar basin, with a 16-metre drill hit returning 2.3 grams per tonne (g/t) gold, 70g/t silver, 1.4 per cent copper and a combined 12.2 per cent lead-zinc from 112m. The stunning reverse-circulation (RC) hole was sweetened by multiple high-grade zones, including a 6-metre core running at 5.2g/t gold, 157g/t silver and a combined 27.9 per cent lead-zinc from 116m. Adding to the intrigue was a separate, copper-rich two-metre kicker grading a hefty 6.2 per cent copper from 123m. Australian Gold and Copper’s Evergreen project in NSW, where recent drilling has returned high-grade polymetallic results. The same hole also produced a shallower intercept of 6m assaying 2g/t gold, 20g/t silver and 0.9 per cent copper from 84m, demonstrating multiple mineralised lenses over more than 220m of strike at the Hillston mineralised zone within Evergreen. Separately, the main Evergreen mineralised zone has been defined over more than 500m of strike. The results form part of the company’s drilling campaign, targeting the high-grade Western Discovery zone at the company’s South Cobar project, as it builds towards a maiden resource estimate for the Evergreen deposit. The standout hole was specifically targeted up-dip and south of a previous discovery hole that returned a 17-metre intercept grading 5.3g/t gold, confirming the system has legs.

Advertisement

′ The high-grade western discovery zone remains open along strike and at depth.′ Australian Gold and Copper managing director Glen Diemar Other notable assay results from the first 18 holes of the 21-hole, 2593-metre RC program add weight to the discovery, showing it is far from a one-hit wonder. One hole returned 9m running 1.6g/t gold and 58g/t silver from 90m, including a higher-grade 5-metre section going 2.4g/t gold and 94g/t silver. Nearby, a further interval yielded 6m grading 1.4g/t gold and 53g/t silver from 95m, featuring a one-metre section of 5.7g/t gold and 202g/t silver. Australian Gold and Copper also reported new assays from previously unsampled historical diamond drill core. A standout hit returned a 7-metre slice of 3.1g/t gold and 18g/t silver from 100m, including a 0.7-metre snippet at a solid 5.9g/t gold. The project sits within a sprawling 2600-square-kilometre landholding in a region known for its world-class deposits. Australian Gold and Copper managing director Glen Diemar said: “This is an exceptional hole. The combination of 6m at 5.2g/t gold, 157g/t silver, 1.0% copper and 27.9% lead-zinc, followed by a copper-rich interval of 2m at 6.2% copper, is an outstanding result at such shallow depths. The high-grade western discovery zone remains open along strike and at depth.” Australian Gold and Copper says its approach is to use broad-spaced drilling to establish the scale of the mineralised system before tightening its focus on the richest and widest zones. The strategy has already served the company well at its Achilles discovery, just 30km away, where an initial 38.5-million-ounce silver-equivalent resource was defined in 2024, with a hefty 58 per cent in the stronger indicated category.

With regulatory approvals now in hand for a third phase of drilling at Evergreen, the rods will be turning again later this quarter. Management says a higher-capacity RC rig is scheduled to arrive to test extensions to the high-grade zones it has just uncovered. In addition, an induced polarisation geophysics survey is underway at the nearby Mount B target, with results pending. Rounding out the portfolio, 230 km to the south, the company holds the Junee project, adding a pure-gold play to its growing stable of precious and base-metal assets. Notably, Australian Gold and Copper remains well-funded to continue its exploration push, with a healthy $5.9 million in cash and no debt as of the end of September. The Evergreen discovery is shaping up to be a significant one for the company. The latest volley of high-grade, polymetallic results from shallow depths confirms a robust mineralising system that appears to remain open along strike and at depth. With a maiden resource estimate for Evergreen on the horizon, assays from three RC holes still pending and a bigger rig on its way to chase the system deeper, Australian Gold and Copper looks likely to give punters plenty of newsflow to watch out for.
