Bulls N’ Bears Big Hits looks at notable drill intercepts reported this week to the ASX. Junior explorers have put on a clinic in how to deliver both sheer grade and massive vertical scale this week, proving that standout drill results can come from everything from a happy geotechnical outcome to deep, multi-horizon sulphide systems. From shallow bonanza gold grades in the Top End and towering porphyry copper columns in southern Peru, through to stacked platinum group metal reefs in WA’s remote West Musgrave, their drill bits have been working overtime across the globe. So let’s dive in. FAR NORTHERN RESOURCES LIMITED (ASX: FNR) Project: Bridge Creek gold project, Northern Territory

Hit: 4m at 110.06g/t gold from 16m downhole Drilling a hole purely for metallurgical and geotechnical testing, only to stumble onto a blistering, shallow bonanza gold zone, is the kind of serendipity every junior explorer dreams about. Far Northern Resources has pulled off that exact coup with one of six diamond drill holes put into its Bridge Creek project, 125 kilometres south-southeast of Darwin in the Northern Territory.

Advertisement

Targeting the northwestern margin of its Bridge Creek Central deposit, where previous drilling had been sparse, the company’s headline hole bored into a high-grade shoot just 16 metres below surface. The intercept returned a remarkable 4-metre length of core grading 110.06 grams per tonne (g/t) gold, underpinned by an eye-watering single-metre chunk assaying 425.2g/t gold from 16m. That’s “thirteen-and-a-half-ounce dirt” in the old prospectors’ language. Immediately above that bonanza zone, the same hole tagged 2m at 14.14g/t gold from 11m, before hitting further mineralised runs of 2m at 1.14g/t gold from 30m and 3m at 3.05g/t gold from 36m. Clocking in at a 440 gram-metre comparative index, the company says that primary intercept is the best one drilled at Bridge Creek to date. And while ground conditions forced the hole to be abandoned at 68.9m, it still gave a last hurrah with 0.9m at 0.83g/t gold from 68m. While the northwestern margin delivered the high-grade fireworks, a second diamond hole pierced straight through the heart of the central deposit to highlight its bulk scale, returning a whopping 60-metre intercept grading 2.0g/t gold from 53m, marking the longest continuous mineralised interval ever drilled at Bridge Creek. Not only did it break the intercept-length record, its broad run was also laced with multiple internal zones, including 7m at 4.13g/t gold from 53m and 28m at 2.10g/t gold from 69m, featuring several single-metre spikes up to 16.41g/t gold.

Advertisement

Situated along the tightly folded axis of the Howley Anticline, roughly 12km north of the historic Cosmopolitan Howley gold mine, the mineralisation sits within quartz-sulphide stockwork zones hosted by black shales and altered dolerites. The latest assays from the six-hole, 584.3-metre diamond campaign will feed straight into a resource upgrade slated for early 2027. Bridge Creek currently hosts 93,000 ounces of gold, forming the backbone of the company’s 117,000-ounce Northern Territory resource base, alongside its nearby Ios project. With the bonanza shoot remaining wide open to the northwest, along strike and down-dip, Far Northern is gearing up for repeat and screen fire assaying on the high-grade core while also planning immediate follow-up drilling ahead of a scoping study later next year. Diamond drill core from AusQuest Limited’s headline hole at the Cangallo project in Peru showing vibrant blue-green oxide chrysocolla and malachite copper mineralisation between 156m and 164m downhole. AUSQUEST LIMITED (ASX: AQD)

Advertisement

Project: Cangallo porphyry copper-gold project, Peru

Hit: 618m at 0.26% copper and 0.06g/t gold from 36m downhole Proving up sheer vertical scale across an emerging porphyry system is the name of the game in South America, and AusQuest Limited has delivered in spades after tagging more than 600 metres of continuous copper-gold mineralisation at its Cangallo project in southern Peru. Positioned 25 kilometres east of the coastal town of Chala, the company’s latest diamond drilling campaign set out to test the depth extent of stockwork veining in the northern sector of the company’s wholly owned prospect. The headline diamond hole stole the show, boring through copper mineralisation from just 36 metres downhole to return a massive 618m run grading 0.26 per cent copper and 0.06g/t gold. That broad envelope was bolstered by several punchier internal intervals, led by a shallow 114-metre zone assaying 0.40 per cent copper and 0.07g/t gold from 88m, alongside deeper hits of 26m at 0.41 per cent copper from 254m and 30m at 0.41 per cent copper from 438m.

Advertisement

A second diamond hole backed up the scale narrative by intersecting an even longer 708-metre zone grading 0.21 per cent copper and 0.05g/t gold from just 4m below surface. It also featured a higher-grade shallow core of 40m going 0.40 per cent copper and 0.11g/t gold from 28m. Other sweeteners in the second hole included 14m assaying 0.35 per cent copper and 0.08g/t gold from 280m; 20m going 0.35 per cent copper and 0.08g/t gold from 438m and 14m running at 0.33 per cent copper and 0.08g/t gold from 538m depth. According to management, the two holes represent the longest copper intercepts reported at Cangallo to date. The most significant copper intercepts across all six holes were accompanied by gold responses up to 0.14g/t, silver to 1.6g/t and molybdenum to 120 parts per million. Interestingly, the system showcases two distinct styles of copper mineralisation. The first is a shallow supergene oxide blanket extending to almost 250m depth, carrying typical secondary-zone chrysocolla and malachite copper mineralisation.

Advertisement

That shallow zone transitions into deeper primary zone stockwork veins loaded with the distinctive copper-iron- sulphide minerals chalcopyrite and bornite, both of which are key ore minerals for copper. Geological mapping indicates the multi-phase intrusive system spans at least 1.5km of strike, with associated dykes stretching beyond 2.5km and remaining wide open. Notably, momentum is also building for the company on the regulatory front, with the Peruvian Government recently declaring Cangallo a project of national interest - a development the company expects will streamline future permitting. With environmental and community approvals already locked in for 20 new drill pads, AusQuest is preparing to mobilise rigs for a stage four reverse circulation program later in the year to test strong surface copper and gold anomalies in the south. TERRA METALS LIMITED (ASX: TM1)

Project: Dante project, Southwest prospect, Western Australia

Advertisement

Hit: 67m at 2.07g/t 3E and 0.13% nickel from 332m downhole Threading a single diamond hole through four stacked mineralised zones while banking project-record platinum group metal grades is a serious statement of intent. Terra Metals has just pulled off that feat at its Southwest discovery in Western Australia’s remote West Musgrave region, where deep drilling continues to unlock a sprawling magmatic sulphide system. Within the company’s wholly owned, 3000-square-kilometre Dante project, the headline diamond hole was designed to test the central block of the Southwest prospect at depth. The hole delivered a standout run of 67m grading 2.07g/t platinum, palladium and gold and 0.13 per cent nickel from 332m downhole. That broad envelope encased an intensely mineralised 31.9-metre zone averaging 3.96g/t platinum, palladium and gold, 0.23 per cent nickel and 0.12 per cent copper from 366m. Boring deeper into the structural reef system revealed even hotter internal spikes, including 8.9m at 11.85g/t platinum, palladium and gold and 0.54 per cent nickel from 389m, including 0.9m assaying 15.86g/t platinum, palladium and gold, 1.84% nickel, 0.13 per cent cobalt and 0.18 per cent copper from 390.4m.

Advertisement

That same 31.9m zone also included 4.7m going 17.90g/t platinum, palladium and gold, 0.36 per cent nickel, 0.19 per cent copper from 393.15m. In a resounding crescendo at 396.8m depth, the drill core delivered a blistering, project record bonanza zone of 1.1m assaying 72.71g/t platinum, palladium and gold - or 2.34 ounces to the tonne - with 0.33 per cent copper and 0.27 per cent nickel. Not to be suppressed too early after that previous headline act, the same hole also intersected three additional mineralised horizons across an eye-watering 452m of drilling, proving that the stacked, near-surface architecture noted in the east plunges cleanly through the central corridor. Above the main zone, the drill bit chewed through a 97.8-metre zone going 1.18g/t platinum, palladium and gold, 0.13 per cent copper and 0.17 per cent nickel from 225.2m, while a deeper slice hit 21m at 1.02g/t platinum, palladium and gold from 520m, including 0.93m at 8.92g/t platinum, palladium and gold and 2.02 per cent nickel. Geologically, the Southwest prospect sits within the Giles Intrusive Complex, with local faulting helping to concentrate high-grade massive and semi-massive sulphides. It lies in the same layered mafic-ultramafic belt that hosts BHP’s massive Nebo-Babel deposit, a magmatic nickel-copper-PGE sulphide system, containing a massive combined 390 million tonne resource grading 0.30 per cent nickel and 0.33 per cent copper. With four drills still at work and more than 35,000m of drill samples from Southwest sitting in the laboratory pipeline, Terra is backed by a hefty $57.9 million cash war chest. Its metallurgical results are due this quarter, ahead of a maiden resource estimate for Southwest early next year and a scoping study slated for mid-year towards a potential prefeasibility study. The head of one of the nation’s largest banks has likened state payroll taxes to “taxing people who give blood” in a full-throated plea to the nation’s politicians to slash red tape and government spending. But the chief executive of Australia’s biggest home lender, Matt Comyn, has cautioned borrowers that interest rates will remain higher as the world deals with the AI construction boom, geopolitical disruption and economic shocks that seem to be accelerating in number. NAB chief executive Andrew Irvine. Alex Ellinghausen NAB boss Andrew Irvine and Comyn gave evidence on Friday to a parliamentary hearing into the banking sector that has been dominated by the state of the economy, government spending and the housing market. The British-Canadian Irvine, who took over as the head of the NAB in 2024, said he continued to be stunned that a country as large as Australia with a population of less than 30 million could have a housing crisis.

Advertisement

“It’s honestly like we’re playing poker with a handful of aces and we’re losing. How is that possible? I find it so disappointing,” he said. Irvine said the level of regulation across the country, especially when it came to construction, was way too high. He then turned his attention to the tax system, particularly state payroll taxes. “[It’s] the most atrocious, abominable tax. It would be like taxing people who give blood,” he said. Irvine said that in the early 2000s, government spending as a share of the economy was a “world-class” 23 per cent. Now it was around 29 per cent which, while lower than most nations, has grown strongly under both sides of politics.

Advertisement

Related Article Big four Cut government spending to reduce inflation: Big banks’ plea He said lower spending, which Treasurer Jim Chalmers has signalled will form a part of his mid-year budget update next month, would take pressure off inflation and interest rates while allowing the private sector to grow. “It is undoubtedly true that additional public sector spending, in an environment where we have poor productive supply capacity, is unhelpful,” Irvine said. “Public spending in and of itself is crowding out private sector spending and that is problematic. I would point out it’s not just the federal government, it’s all levels of government, state government, local councils, it’s everything.” Comyn noted that lower government spending would reduce inflation pressures across the country, but warned it would not be a panacea for all the issues facing Australia.

Advertisement

He said the surge in spending in areas such as AI meant the very low interest rates of the 2010s – when the cash rate in Australia fell to 0.75 per cent ahead of the pandemic – were gone. “The outlook for interest rates is higher than it has been for the past decade,” he said. Comyn said while Australian government debt – which on Friday fell below $1 trillion – was much lower than most other nations, it was important for fiscal discipline. CBA chief executive Matt Comyn says shocks to the global economy are growing in number. Alex Ellinghausen He said a suite of policy reforms were needed to boost productivity which would then help Australia deal with an increasingly shock-prone global economy that was straining under pressures stretching from the AI construction boom to demographic change to geopolitical tensions.

Advertisement

“I think the structural forces that are shaping geopolitics make it far less predictable,” he said. Related Article Negative gearing Record plunge in investor loans as tax overhaul hits property market “Living within your means as a company and country is important … there are much more significant and more frequent shocks likely to affect the economy.” Comyn also suggested the Reserve Bank, which has lifted the cash rate five times this year, may have erred in cutting interest rates last year, saying it could have waited longer to ensure inflation was going to stay within its 2-3 per cent target band before easing monetary policy. Westpac’s chief economist, Luci Ellis, on Friday said the RBA may be done with interest rate rises as the economy slows more quickly than anticipated by the Reserve.

Advertisement

She said the fallout from this year’s steep fall in house prices would weigh on the broader economy and inflation well into next year. The recent drop in oil prices, which are now below what the RBA forecast only a week ago, would also aid in reducing price pressures across Australia. “[Monetary] policy is clearly restrictive, and the risk of overdoing the inflation correction is growing,” she said. Markets opened with a spring in their step this week, only to finish flat on their backs again. Oil took the first hit as hopes of an end to the war in Iran sent barrel prices tumbling from around US$100 to below US$90 for the first time since August...that’s before President Donald Trump grabbed the brake lever on Thursday, shouting “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed.” This week’s Bulls N’ Bears Runner of the Week is… G8 Education. The orange leader of the free world continued, stating that the US had hundreds of billions of dollars of frozen overseas Iranian regime money and that the US in fact controlled the Strait. The Brent price suggested otherwise, bouncing back to almost US$96 in a serious rollercoaster of a week. Inflation fears were quick to follow as hot US cost-of-living data mixed with oil had the punters betting on a December Fed rate hike, leaving bond yields uncomfortably close to five per cent and the US dollar surging once again. Gold, in turn, handed last week’s rally straight back, slipping below US$4000 and shedding nearly three per cent overnight to around US$3880.

Advertisement

Bad news flowing from the Middle East left AI as the last shiny hope and for a few days, Wall Street delivered. Fresh from last week’s US$3.2 trillion rout, tech roared back. Then Jensen Huang’s wandering eyes got involved. Nvidia’s chief admitted an extramarital affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, prompting the board to investigate whether he had been the “target of a foreign intelligence effort”. Reports linked the woman to Megaspeed, Nvidia’s biggest Southeast Asian customer, which was already accused of “chip smuggling.” The world’s biggest company proceeded to shed more than US$427 billion (A$627 billion) in two sessions - the most expensive affair since Helen of Troy. Then came Wednesday night’s twist: The New York Times reported a second alleged affair, this time with a senior Nvidia executive, while The Wall Street Journal said the board was preparing to show him the door. By Thursday, a reported third dalliance had emerged, and shares in the world’s biggest company were down 20 per cent in a little over a week… oooft.

Back home, everyday Australians continue to feel the hurt, with consumer sentiment at a four-year low, rates at an 18-year high and mortgage holders’ mood plunging alongside their housing prices. And the reward for all that government-induced inflation? A parade of praise for Dr Jim Chalmers. With calls for his resignation growing louder, Labour lined up to slap him on the back. Albo declared the Treasurer was “doing a great job” – at raising revenues - and that he wanted him by his side. Standing by your man is a fine quality in a mate, but not when it’s at the cost of tens of millions of people across the country, I’d wager. Meanwhile, Usman Khawaja was busy standing by his Australian cricketing brethren in a different way this week. Waiting beside them at the bus stop to throw his old teammates under the wheels, it seems, for a more personal form of revenue raising in his latest autobiography. His claim that ‘Sandpapergate’ went well beyond the three players who were banned was a great way to honour the Baggy Green, with his dirty gossip rag – biography – set to hit shelves just in time for Christmas. Finally, the market mayhem week looked like it might come to an end, only for Australians to wake Friday morning to Microsoft’s entire office offering on the fritz, with Outlook and Teams remaining down throughout the business day. Business was at a standstill, with nowhere more evident than the market overlords down at the ASX, who certainly didn’t have the answers. Outlook’s outage sent the ASX’s archaic system scrambling, as a grand total of just 180 announcements made it out on Friday, a fraction of the usual 550ish daily haul.

Last week it was fridges frying; this week it’s Outlook dying - and the consequences of a major technology outage are flooding across the market. title: The Microsoft outage is part of a growing trend. This is how to prepare for further disruption
text:
Today's Microsoft outage has highlighted the risks of relying on cloud-based communications and Australians should be expecting more disruptions in the future, one expert says.

RMIT Associate Professor of engineering Mark Gregory says companies are not applying best practice in their processes.

"If we look at the outages that have occurred with Optus and Telstra, and also Vodafone, in some way they've all related back to a reduction in the amount of funds being put into the engineering side of the business," he said.

"So that when equipment goes down, or it's misconfigured, you then end up with a catastrophic outcome."

A major Telstra mobile outage in July that sparked chaos, with Triple Zero calls and businesses affected, was linked to the failure to maintain ageing equipment.

Gregory said engineering processes developed over hundreds of years generally follow a path of testing, checking with small groups, small pilot platforms and testing again before changes are rolled out.

"But that process is often either not used, or it's shortened because of the timelines that companies place on their engineering teams."

The Microsoft outage on Friday disrupted the use of popular programs such as Outlook and impacted the Australian Federal Police and Australian Security Intelligence Organisation.

Microsoft reported a widespread outage on Friday that left users unable to access Outlook, Teams and other Microsoft services. Source: Getty / Scott Olson

Gregory said a network misconfiguration — when settings don't match what the network expects — appears to have resulted in some cloud servers being disconnected from Outlook.

"Unbelieveably, they've had to reboot them to get them to rejoin the cloud," Gregory said.

He said businesses are trying to speed up the process of making changes, updates or improvements to their software and systems, and this is coming at a cost.

"The updates have been coming very quickly nowadays compared with what we experienced 10 or 15 years ago."

These frequent updates, along with increasing hacking attacks, have seen a rise in outages in recent years, but there are actions businesses and individuals can take to minimise the disruption.

What can Australians do?

Gregory said companies in Australia have already been advised to plan for national outages of telephone networks after a series of failures.

"So if you're a Telstra customer, you need to have an Optus SIM card or something on another network as a backup."

It's also important for companies, businesses, individuals and families to also have backups of software systems so that alternatives are available when one system fails.

"If you're an Outlook or Microsoft user, you keep a Google or Gmail account as a backup so that you're still able to communicate or receive emails," Gregory said.

Software is increasingly connected to cloud servers and he said businesses should also consider backups for human resource progams, billing, invoicing and accounting software.

"Unfortunately, I see many businesses that are not prepared to look at having that redundancy or backup approaches, and they simply rely upon everything being available," he said.

"And when it's not, their staff are really just being left in limbo.

The worst possible outcome is where companies order staff to take leave, which some of them do.

"Therefore, the problem becomes one that the staff have to carry."

In the past, businesses stored data and software programs within their own systems and offices.

"Due to the cost of doing that, over time companies have migrated their email into the cloud to use Office 365 or other hosted solutions," he said.

But Gregory said businesses are starting to understand the importance of having greater control over their services.

Businesses are increasing relying on cloud services rather than storing data and systems on their own in-house servers. Source: Getty / Jetta Productions Inc

"If you have your systems and services being provided from a long way away, such as the United States or Asia, the chances of failure increase," he said.

"'[Locating] them locally — such as within their own business or within the cloud situated in Sydney or Melbourne or Brisbane — you do see less outages when that occurs."

The advantage of this approach could be seen during the Microsoft outage as businesses whose emails were hosted by a company separate to the Microsoft Exchange Online, were still able to use programs such as Outlook despite the wider disruption.

'Part of our daily lives'

SBS has previously spoken to experts who say it's time for individuals and businesses to stop putting so much data and other information online, but Gregory said the computerisation of business processes is probably not going to change.

"It's a typical part of our daily lives today," he said.

"The question for many organisations has to be whether they rely solely upon cloud solution providers, or do they utilise alternative approaches such as self-hosted [services] or having those software packages run within the organisation."

Gregory said organisations need to work out the best options for themselves so they can still operate when these incidents occur.

"The only downside of course is cost," he said.

"You're paying for this alternative solution. [But] it's very difficult for companies to have hundreds or thousands of staff sitting around looking at computers unable to do anything, it's not productive.

Gregory says organisations also need address hacking attacks, which are on the rise partly because AI is making them easier.

"Nearly every major organisation in Australia has been hacked," he said.

"Quite often it's been because of a reluctance by the management teams and those organisations to actually spend the money that's needed to protect the company from hackers."

He believes the fines for failing to adopt best practice approaches are very low, and so companies were still underspending.

"The next phase will be class actions and people suing companies for losing their personal data," he said.

"And we really need to see more of that because Australia is still being hacked too often."

title: Cricket's war of words ramps up as Warner claims Khawaja was thrown 'under the bus'
text:
In brief Sandpapergate reemerged this week after Usman Khawaja claimed the entire team knew about the 2018 ball-tampering plot.

Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins denied the allegations, prompting a rebuke from David Warner.

Former cricketer David Warner has accused Pat Cummins of throwing Usman Khawaja "under the bus" after the Australian cricket captain rejected claims that the whole team was aware of the 2018 ball-tampering plot.

During a 70-minute press conference on Friday morning, Cummins broke his silence about sandpapergate, saying Khawaja's version of events was "complete and utter nonsense".

The scandal resurfaced this week after Khawaja, who retired from international cricket in January, claimed in his new autobiography, Sabr, that the entire team knew about ball tampering during the third Test match against South Africa in Cape Town in 2018.

The allegations contradict the findings of a Cricket Australia investigation, which found Cameron Bancroft, who was filmed placing sandpaper down his cricket pants on the field, Steve Smith and Warner were the only ones involved in the ball-tampering, and it was a one-off incident.

The trio were subsequently suspended and fined.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Warner, who earlier this week said Khawaja's claims were "100 per cent accurate", on Friday defended Khawaja and hit back at Cummins.

"I still stick by Uzzie and what he's written in that book, because it is the truth, and I really, really support him," Warner said on Fox Cricket.

"I actually feel for him at the moment. I actually feel that today, the captain threw Uzzie under the bus, and I’m very, very disappointed about that.

"All three of us [Warner, Bancroft, Smith] have paid a big price in this thing. I hadn’t spoken about it in eight years, but at the end of the day, we’ve got to live with these consequences daily. We've been served a life punishment."

Warner stood by his claim that the Cricket Australia investigation had been mismanaged.

"The way it was handled in the first place, it was hard for us to go back and give more evidence. I feel like it was a botched investigation," he said.

"It was a quick one to get it over and done with. Some of the questions were quite challenging in the way it was being planted on us, and we had to move on and just accept responsibility, the three of us, and we ultimately did.

"We don't have that opportunity to go there and speak again. [Cricket Australia CEO] Todd Greenberg squashed that the other day. There probably are going to be conversations behind the scenes after this."

Warner later added he would one day tell his side of the story and he was "not going to accept until the truth is out there".

Cricket Australia has stood by its findings, with Greenberg saying on Tuesday it would not reopen the investigation.

Khawaja has faced criticism over the timing of his allegations, which coincide with the release of his book.

Cummins: 'Complete and utter nonsense'

Earlier on Friday, Cummins rejected Khawja's claims, saying: "When [Usman Khawaja] says we all knew, if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out in the field, he's 100 per cent wrong."

"I have said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening, but I think Usman actually says things that are actually far more serious than that."

He also alleged there had been ball tampering during an earlier match.

Cummins said those claims were "complete and utter nonsense".

Cummins said Khawaja was a friend but "friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations".

"In his book, Uzzie's been casual with my life and the lives of many others, and I think Australian cricket. I support his right to tell his story 100 per cent," he said.

"I'm really glad that he feels like he can. But we have to be accountable for the things that we say and do."

Khawaja said in his book that he told Bancroft to be careful and avoid being scapegoated when the scandal unfolded.

"I was genuinely shocked this week when I found out that Usman admitted that he told Cam [Bancroft] to be careful when using sandpaper," he said.

"That's not the Usman that I know. It's not the Usman ... that has been part of a team that's helped rebuild this Australian cricket culture over the last eight years."

Cummins said the culture of the 2018 side was very different to the current team.

"At that stage I think [the side] had a win-at-all-costs mentality, had an ugly underbelly, and there were too many silos within the team," he said.

"Traits that I hope that everyone's seen, and I try very hard to eradicate for the last six years as captain."

Some claims 'probably defamatory'

Cummins said he had received advice some of the claims were "probably defamatory" but he would not be taking any legal action.

"You got to move on. It's been eight years," he said.

"You got to draw a line at some point."

Cummins said parts of Khawaja's allegations were likely true but other parts were "vague".

"Some of these things are probably true, and they are his accounts of what happened. But I think there's a few big leaps here where he's being vague and I think the details really matter in that difference," he said.

"Perhaps there was conversations with Cameron Bancroft around taking sandpaper out and how to do it. That doesn't mean that everyone in that dressing room knew what was going on.

"The way he's presented his story, I think he's done it in a very casual manner, and it affects a lot of people. That's what I'm grappling with at the moment because I don't think it's okay."

Cummins saw ball-tampering in Sheffield Shield match

Cummins said the only other time he saw illegal ball-tampering was during a Sheffield Shield match, when a senior batter, who he chose not to name, brought a bottle cap onto the pitch.

"It was dealt with. The umpires knew it as well. They caught him out and said, 'You've got to stop that right now.' It was dealt with. That's the only time I had seen something illegal out there," he said.

Cummins has also addressed footage published by The Australian newspaper on Thursday of what appeared to be a heated argument with his wife.

"We weren't having a spat. Becky was very frustrated, animated, and really not happy with Usman," he said.

"It's half very comical. Becky wears her heart on her sleeve. And half all a bit ridiculous, isn't it? We are here talking about something that was dealt with eight-and-a-half years ago.

"Now I'm walking my one-and-a-half-year-old daughter with nappies out the front and I got cameras chasing me and my family. For me, that's a bit ridiculous."

Others from the 2018 side have also issued denials.

Australian fast bowler Mitchell Starc, who in 2021 stated he had no knowledge of the ball-tampering, said on Tuesday his recollection had not changed.

Mitch Marsh, who was part of the 2018 side, refused to answer questions on Wednesday about the allegations.

"There has obviously been a lot of noise around this week and I respect that certain people have told their stories, but I’m not here to share mine today."

title: 'Even a snail would agree': Greta Thunberg takes aim at Australia
text:
In Brief Greta Thunberg addressed a crowd at the UN climate summit in Türkiye on Thursday.

After not appearing at previous COP events, the activist said she returned to call for urgent action.

Environmental activist Greta Thunberg has slammed Australia's track record on climate action at COP31 talks in Türkiye, saying "even a snail would agree" that the country needs to move faster.

The 23-year-old's appearance alongside speakers from Australia, Nepal, Rwanda and Gaza caused traffic chaos inside the United Nations' climate summit in Antalya on Thursday, which also heard criticism of Australia's ongoing mining approvals.

Australia's Energy Minister Chris Bowen will lead negotiations at the annual event, which has drawn more than 92,000 attendees, and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese arrived on Wednesday for the leaders' summit portion of the event.

Asked whether she agreed with comments about Australia's slow record on climate action, Thunberg said her opinion was obvious.

"Even a snail would agree with that," she told the crowd.

"It's common sense. It doesn't get more clear than that."

Thunberg previously spoke at the event in 2018 and 2019 but criticised the COP26 event in 2021, describing it as "blah, blah, blah".

She returned this year to bring attention to the state of the climate, she said, and call for action to prevent further disasters.

"We are all here because we know that the climate crisis is already here and now, and it is already a matter of life and death," Thunberg said.

"And these disastrous trends we are seeing unfold all over the world are going to continue to exponentially get worse and worse.

"We have to start acting accordingly."

Indigenous woman Rikki Dank also spoke at the event, saying Albanese should listen to calls from Traditional Owners to stop approving new and extended fossil fuel projects.

"He needs to stop speaking and start listening to the Australian people when they say no more new coal, oil and gas," she said.

Albanese and Bowen have so far declined to address proposals to transition away from fossil fuels at the COP31 event, instead discussing electrification and renewable energy targets.

title: Nvidia CEO quits following affair allegations involving suspected spy
text:
In brief Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang is stepping down following allegations he had an affair with a suspected spy.

The departure could also have far-reaching consequences for US chip export policy.

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang is stepping down, leaving the artificial intelligence industry without its biggest champion and clouding the future of the chip maker he built into an AI powerhouse.

Chief financial officer Colette Kress will take over as interim chief executive as ‌Nvidia looks for a permanent successor, the US company said on Thursday.

It named former Synopysys chief executive and board member Harvey Jones as its first-ever board chairman.

Huang, ‌who co-founded Nvidia and is its fourth-largest investor with a stake of about 3.61 per cent, will exit the board as well.

Nvidia shares in the US fell more than 14 per cent at the opening bell on Thursday, before recovering to a decline of about 5 per cent.

Suspected spy scandal

Pressure had been mounting on Huang in recent days after reports said the 63-year-old, who is married, had an affair with businesswoman Alice Huang, who US authorities suspect of spying for China.

Nvidia's board met on Wednesday to consider removing him, a person familiar with the matter said, after reports earlier in the day that Huang also had an extramarital affair with a senior company executive who reported to him.

Nvidia's chips dominate the data centres that train and run AI systems, placing it at the centre of both the US-China technology race and a massive wave of investment reshaping the US economy.

The company also invests some of its billions in profits in other AI firms that in turn buy its chips, raising the stakes for the wider tech sector.

The departure could also have far-reaching consequences for US chip export policy, given Huang's push to preserve access to the Chinese market and his close ties with US President Donald Trump.

Revelations that US intelligence was investigating Alice Huang for facilitating shipments of Nvidia chips to Chinese firms set off a series of events.

Wall Street began raising questions about Nvidia's governance and Jensen Huang's personal conduct while the company's board launched an internal investigation and hired outside counsel.

US politicians also began to push for tighter curbs on chip exports to China.

Chinese authorities have denied the allegations.

Alice Huang is currently living in Beijing with the knowledge of security officials, Bloomberg ⁠News reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said in Beijing on Thursday that the US should stop making up "so-called spy stories" to justify technology blockades.

The leadership upheaval comes just days before investors are set to hear from Nvidia on its financial performance and outlook, with its quarterly ‌results due on November 17.

Earlier on Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang had also had an extramarital affair with a company executive who reported to him.

The relationship was with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, the New York Times said, citing five people who worked at the company.

title: These Australians lost their jobs. Here's what they're facing now
text:
IN BRIEF More than 108,000 people were retrenched in July and August, according to the ABS.

Experts say AI can be both a help and a hindrance in job hunting.

For four years, Saskia Tjahja worked to help people with disabilities enjoy playing football — a job she "loved" because of the difference it made.

But in mid-September, it was all taken away. Her position was made redundant.

"It's been really tough because obviously I really loved working there and I loved what I do," the Perth-based marketing communications and events manager told SBS News.

"It was really difficult to say goodbye."

And now, two months after losing her job, she is facing an "anxiety-inducing" environment as "people are struggling to get jobs".

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

While Tjahja's role was made redundant for reasons specific to her employer, she is among many Australians now looking for work amid a broader wave of job cuts across the economy. In recent months, redundancies have been most acute in banking and finance, technology and professional services.

The latest data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) shows that 108,300 people were retrenched in July and August; if September's numbers are similar, the quarterly retrenchment number will be the highest since August 2021.

The country's unemployment rate also climbed to 4.7 per cent in September, the highest level since October 2021, according to the ABS.

But the job-hunting process is not like it used to be — at least for Tjahja.

"I started immediately looking for jobs and applying for jobs. However, I've only been contacted once by a potential job opportunity, but I turned that down," she said.

Tjahja said that, with her previous experience, usually "it takes three months" for her to find a job, but this time she does not have "high expectations".

And in her job-hunting experience, she is not alone.

'Unsure about my future'

SEEK, an employment listings platform, also said its job ads rose slightly by about 0.6 per cent in September.

The number of applications for each job has been rising consistently and rose by 1.7 per cent in September.

Blair Chapman, SEEK chief economist, said the numbers mean "job seekers are facing greater competition for available roles, which can make the job hunting process more difficult", adding Australia’s "job market remains competitive".

Copywriter Erin Arnett has been navigating this tough job market for nearly a year.

She lost her job in January and has been applying for a handful of jobs each month since then, but she still hasn’t found one.

"It's been pretty hard, because previously when I've looked for work, I've been able to find something within two or three months, but it's been, well, all year, " Arnett said.

Erin Arnett is still searching for work, almost a year after being laid off from her last job. Credit: Supplied

"It's pretty disheartening not being able to find something and not being sure when you're going to find something.

"It's leaving me very unsure about my future, and I'm not entirely sure what my next move should be."

LinkedIn data shows almost 70 per cent of Australians believe finding a job has become harder over the past year. The platform's figures suggest that perception reflects a more competitive market, with the number of applicants per role nearly doubling since early 2022 while hiring rates in Australia have fallen by 21 per cent.

LinkedIn career expert Brendan Wong said two main factors are behind the tough job-hunting environment.

"I would say a challenging economy and the introduction of AI (artificial intelligence) are rapidly changing the face of work, and companies are having to respond," he told SBS News.

Recent ABS data also shows that, in the previous year, job seekers said their main difficulty in finding a job was that there were "too many applicants for available jobs".

AI applications

A higher number of applicants per job also complicates the process for employers.

Matthew Dickerson, Asia Pacific CEO of the global recruitment firm Hays, told SBS News this is partly related to AI, which helps candidates apply for "more jobs and customise their CVs at scale".

"As a result, working through that from an employer's perspective to find good [candidates] has become harder, because a lot more of the CVs look very good because AI has helped write those," he said.

"At the same time, the nature of the roles is changing slightly. And so employers are looking for newer skills ... For example, they're looking for people who've got demonstrable AI capability in the job.

READ MORE See the full list: The jobs Australian employers are struggling most to fill

According to LinkedIn, 77 per cent of recruiters say it's harder to find qualified talent than it was a year ago, up from 68 per cent the year before.

Dickerson said the growing use of AI in job applications has also made recruitment more time-consuming,

"They're having to actually do a lot more in-person screening with the potential employees to be able to find the people that best meet their requirements," he said

The human edge in a competitive job market

While AI is changing how employers assess candidates, Wong suggests a human touch could help candidates improve their chances in the country's job market.

"Relationships are pivotal to getting a foot in the door. It could be as simple as starting with the people that they know already," he said.

"Begin with a small interaction. It can be just sending out a message — reaching out to maybe have a coffee."

LinkedIn data shows that Australian applicants with an inside connection at a company are 4.5 times more likely to be hired than those without one.

Wong also cautions against relying too heavily on AI to write CVs and cover letters.

"The trick is to make sure that you're not just copying and pasting whatever the AI is coming up with, because everyone is starting to sound very similar," Wong said.

"Everyone is using the same kind of language, so to stand out, people really have to hone in on what makes them different."

Experts suggest looking into other industries might also help.

Chapman from SEEK said "there are still opportunities for job seekers across the labour market" and "in September, we saw growth in industries such as retail and consumer products and hospitality and tourism, while mining, resources and energy, engineering and construction recorded some of the strongest annual growth in job ads".

title: House price falls haven't made homes more affordable, inquiry told, as banks grilled on profits
text:
IN BRIEF Westpac says construction lending has fallen 30 per cent, as high costs deter new housing projects.

Housing affordability has reportedly worsened despite falling prices, with prices forecast to drop until 2028.

The government's housing policy changes and interest rate rises have not led to more affordable homes or an increase in housing supply, but prices are tipped to continue falling until 2028, a parliamentary inquiry into Australia's four biggest banks heard on Thursday.

Westpac is lending to 30 per cent fewer housing construction projects than it did up to a year and a half ago, its chief told a parliamentary inquiry on Thursday.

The bank was careful not to pin the tailspin on the government's abolition of negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount in the federal budget in May, chalking it up mainly to cost pressures.

Labor's reforms included a carve-out letting investors negatively gear new builds — meant to incentivise construction investment — but Westpac chief executive Anthony Miller said Westpac was yet to see that take shape.

"There is some improvement in that area, but it has not come through as fast or as significant as perhaps we would like," Miller said.

He said governments still needed to work harder to spur new building investment, boost supply and improve housing affordability.

"Providing more resource for the demand side isn't going to solve the problem," he said.

The day before Thursday's hearings, it was revealed investor home loans had cratered by a record 30.6 per cent in the year to September.

READ MORE The type of homeowners on the rise as fewer Australians take out a mortgage

Labor hailed the crash as a win for first home-buyers because it showed speculators were retreating from the market much faster than owner-occupiers.

It also cheered an uptick in the volume of investor loans going to new builds, which jumped from 17 to 28 per cent between the March and September quarters.

Banks grilled over interest-rate profits

Inquiry chair Ed Husic said everyone in Australia seemed to be going through tough times, except for big businesses, with banks making close to $300,000 profit from the average owner-occupier 30-year home loan, a profit that is up $40,000 since interest rates began rising earlier this year.

"A big four bank is making a profit of $234 a week off an average Australian family with an average loan," the Labor MP said.

But ANZ Group CEO Nuno Matos disputed those numbers, saying banks are "performing their role in delivering to society" and "the mortgage business is one of the least profitable businesses in banking in Australia, and it has reduced profitability year after year, at least in the last 20 years".

"All Australians are feeling the pressures of the cost of living. That means inflation is high and interest rates are high, which is not improving the quality of lives of Australians," Matos said.

READ MORE See the full list: The suburbs where home prices have grown as much as 417 per cent

He said ANZ is not taking advantage of that, but merely "doing our job".

The bank expects home prices to fall about 13.5 per cent from peak to trough and stabilise in 2028.

He warned the economy is in a "dangerous situation" as governments and companies fight for capital to build artificial intelligence, defence capability, energy projects or deal with government budget deficits at the same time as interest rates start climbing.

"They are contributing to a competition for capital. We never saw this amount of spending in our lives, in our lifetimes," he said.

Liberal MP Simon Kennedy said housing has "actually become less affordable in the last 12 months, 5.4 per cent less according to the HIA (Housing Industry Association), despite housing [prices] going down 8 per cent, and then government spending at a 40-year high is adding to this interest rate pressure, which is making housing less affordable".

Westpac highlights supply constraints

Westpac said the government's policies had largely failed to boost home building.

While the bank's lending for new housing construction was higher this year than last year, Westpac says higher construction, labour, and material costs meant builders only constructed 5,300 apartments and townhouses this year, down from 8,000 last year — a 30 per cent decline.

"Higher construction costs are making affordable apartments and townhouses less attractive to build than higher-end dwellings," Miller said.

"The longer-term challenge remains supply — particularly the supply of affordable housing. Australia is simply not building enough housing to meet demand," Miller said.

He also urged the federal government to make a "break-glass decision" and fix the planning system and slow approval processes.

"It's an anchor on our growth. We will not meet our targets on housing or energy nor will we improve living standards unless we move faster," he said.

Meanwhile, mortgage arrears and hardship are rising among ANZ customers — with hardship hitting five in 1,000 customers, up about 10 per cent in six months — and arrears are expected to worsen before improving.

The bank reported loan applications fell 12 per cent over six months, with investor applications down 27 per cent and owner-occupier applications roughly flat.

title: See the full list: The suburbs where home prices have grown as much as 417 per cent
text:
In Brief Median sale prices have doubled from metropolitan Sydney and Darwin through to coastal cities and regional towns.

Suburbs along the east coast represent the largest growth in value for houses and units.

In 2011, Australia's property market was valued at around $4.2 trillion.

Fifteen years later, it's worth more than $12 trillion, according to the latest update from the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

But growth in property value has varied largely due to lifestyle factors and development booms, analysis by real estate advertiser REA Group on prices since 2011 shows.

In Pokolbin, in NSW's Hunter Valley region, the median house price in 2011 was $315,000. Now, it sits at $1,628,000, having risen 417 per cent.

Rounding out the top 10 behind Pokolbin, the suburbs with the largest growth in median sale prices for houses across the country are Jordan Springs (NSW), Palm Beach (NSW), Byron Bay (NSW), Mermaid Waters (QLD), Bellamack (NT), Boolaroo (NSW), Buddina (QLD), Miami (QLD) and Forde (ACT).

The east coast also leads the top suburbs for units.

The largest growth has been in Palm Beach (QLD), Bogangar (NSW), Tugun (QLD), Jindabyne (NSW), Miami (QLD), Reedy Creek (QLD), Mona Vale (NSW), Currumbin Waters (QLD), Double Bay (NSW) and Casuarina (NSW).

In the Gold Coast's Palm Beach, the median sale price for a unit is $1.2 million, an increase of 260 per cent from its value 15 years ago. Similar growth has been seen in suburbs along the Gold Coast.

The Northern Territory tended to record smaller price growth for units than for houses, with the top suburb increasing 26 per cent over the period.

READ MORE Buying a unit is cheaper than renting in this inner-city spot

Trends across the country

From metropolitan Sydney and Darwin to coastal cities and regional towns, median sale prices have doubled in dozens of suburbs over the last 15 years.

Megan Lieu, a senior economic analyst at REA Group, says several factors have driven this growth.

"One of the key factors has been the lower cash rates seen throughout 2012-2021," she told SBS News.

"Borrowing capacities increased, resulting in higher demand from buyers and significant growth in home prices."

The majority of suburbs in the top 10 are in NSW and Queensland.

Lifestyle factors have also been a major driver.

"Any beachside, coastal and tree-change suburbs saw strong growth in the past 15 years as well," Lieu said.

"With Australia's population ageing, many retirees or older Australians have also migrated to Queensland, in particular the Richmond–Tweed, Sunshine Coast and Gold Coast regions where lifestyle and community meet."

There has been strong interstate migration, with many residents from NSW and Victoria choosing to move to Queensland in particular.

For other suburbs, their recent development contributes to the growth, such as Jordan Springs, which was only officially registered in 2011.

In the Northern Territory, suburbs like Bellamack and Johnston have jumped much higher than the rest of the state, with 313 per cent and 260 per cent growth respectively. The next highest suburb grew in value by 69 per cent.

"With affordability becoming more challenged, many Australians have moved away from metro areas, where homes tend to cost more," Lieu said.

"This has driven strong population growth in regional areas and higher rates of growth in these areas compared to capital cities. Unsurprisingly, the majority of the top 10 growth suburbs nationally were located in regional areas."

title: Facing fossil fuel criticism, Albanese urges world not to overlook Pacific climate plight
text:
In brief Anthony Albanese has called for nations to support the Pacific Resilience Facility initiative, launched in 2025.

UN secretary-general António Guterres railed against the oil and gas lobby during his speech at COP31.

World leaders have been urged to extend a lifeline to Pacific nations under threat from rising sea levels and extreme weather at the COP31 summit in Türkiye.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese issued the call to action on Wednesday at the opening of the two-day World Leaders Climate Action Summit segment of the United Nations event.

Australia will lead negotiations at the annual climate talks and Albanese said it would use the opportunity to highlight the plight of its regional neighbours.

"We sought this role because we wanted to speak for the people of the world who need urgent action, including those from our Pacific family," he said.

He also called for nations to support the Pacific Resilience Facility, launched in 2025 and designed to raise $US500 million ($726 million) for climate change and adaptation projects.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"I plead with you to join our campaign to help the nations of the Pacific to confront a climate challenge that they certainly did not create," he said.

However, climate activists and politicians have criticised Albanese for failing to directly mention fossil fuels during his speech.

Independent senator David Pocock said that, while Australia has some "good stories" to tell when it comes to adopting renewable energy, more work is needed to reduce Australia's involvement in fossil fuel projects.

"The fact that the prime minister not once mentioned fossil fuels, I think, shows you how captured the major parties are by the fossil fuel industry," Pocock told SBS News.

"They want to be able to talk about the good stuff we're doing, but not the fact that the Albanese government has approved 38 fossil fuel projects, new projects or extensions since they came into office, and that is not compatible with a livable Pacific, let alone what's happening here in Australia."

READ MORE A rare climate milestone arrives as a four-year deadline looms

Pocock said Australia needs to "get real" about weaning itself off of its dependency on fossil fuels.

"This is a huge issue. It's here now. It's only getting worse, unless we see countries like Australia ... the third biggest fossil fuel exporter of the world, come up with a very serious plan going forward around not approving more fossil fuel projects and a planned phase-out."

'The world we know is over'

Marshall Islands President Hilda Heine, whose Pacific nation is threatened by rising sea levels, said: "Every new oil well drilled, every new piece of coal extracted is a threat to my country's future."

"The discovery of new fossil fuel resources is not something to celebrate, but something to fear," she said.

Heine also warned of the dire threat posed by overshooting the 2015 Paris Agreement to hold "the increase in the global average temperature to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels" and pursue efforts "to limit the temperature increase to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels".

"It's time to wake up," said Heine. "Our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming, or the world we know is over."

Outgoing United Nations secretary-general António Guterres also addressed attendees, calling for urgent action to address climate change, including phasing out fossil fuels.

His call came months after the UN warned the world was on track to surpass 1.5C of warming within a few years and should act to limit the severity and duration of the overshoot.

"Our first climate duty is to tell the truth, and the brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us," he said.

"The last four years were the hottest ever, and fossil fuel interests keep making a killing while killing our planet. This is the path of mutually assured destruction."

Greater investments in renewable energy, including solar power, could help nations move away from coal, oil and gas, Guterres said.

"Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs, but that will not happen on its own."

"It's time to kick the habit and end the fossil-fuel addiction," he said, adding "that means no new coal, no new oil and gas infrastructure that puts 1.5 degrees further out of reach".

Those comments were seized on by former Greens leader Adam Bandt — who is attending COP31 as chief executive of the Australian Conservation Foundation — who called them "a very significant intervention" and told reporters Australia and other nations were being "called out" on the issue.

"We want to see Australia up on that stage saying that they're not going to open up new coal and gas mines," he said.

title: Finnish president brings Albanese into embassy joke that's swept the world
text:
In brief Finland's Canberra embassy made an innocuous post on its Instagram page earlier this week announcing a one-day closure.

The mundane announcement took on a life of its own, receiving more than 11 million views.

An innocuous social media post by Finland's embassy in Canberra has become an unlikely viral meme, attracting millions of views and reaching the highest levels of government in both countries.

"I have confirmed to the Prime Minister of Australia Anthony Albanese that the Finnish Embassy in Canberra is open," Finnish President Alexander Stubb said in a selfie posted with Albanese at the COP31 climate summit in Türkiye on Thursday morning AEDT.

The president was referring to an announcement three days earlier by the Finnish embassy in Canberra that it would be closed on Tuesday for a team planning event.

Set to a jaunty piano tune and accompanied by a video of the northern lights, the post was simply a light-hearted public service announcement.

But thanks to the unpredictable nature of social media algorithms, the seemingly mundane announcement took on a life of its own, attracting more than 11 million views on Instagram and hundreds of thousands of likes.

Social media users were quick to embrace the meme, flooding the comments section with tongue-in-cheek responses.

"Bad day to be a Finnish embassy in Canberra enthusiast," one said.

"Is everything ok? Call if you need me," said another.

Other Finnish embassies also joined in on the joke.

"For anyone affected by this closure, the Embassy of Finland in Prague will be open as usual tomorrow," the Czech Republic embassy said.

Finland's ambassador to Australia, Arto Haapea, said the embassy was taking the viral moment in its stride.

"We started the planning day quite normally. We went through what a successful year we had this year, all the visits and then how do we build on that for next year," he told ABC News breakfast on Thursday.

"Then people started getting messages like, hang on, there's something happening on Instagram and elsewhere."

He said the response had been overwhelmingly positive.

"Everybody was saying that Finland has never been this big in the news. The other thing, Canberra has never been this big on the market either; maybe it's a positive for everyone," he said.

The embassy followed up with a tongue-in-cheek ribbon-cutting ceremony on Wednesday to mark the reopening.

"After 24 harrowing hours, international expressions of grief and an unprecedented outpouring of solidarity, the Embassy of Finland in Canberra has officially reopened after its temporary closure on 10 November 2026," it said on social media.

Previous posts by the page had attracted fewer than 100 likes, but Haapea said the embassy was now attracting real-life visitors.

"Yesterday there was actually a fair bit of traffic outside the embassy, lots of people were coming to take pictures and we put some brochures outside to make sure we spread the Finnish propaganda at the same time. That was all good," he said.

It's not the first time Finland has found itself in the social media spotlight.

Last month, the country's state-owned tourism agency launched a viral campaign inviting 16 singles from around the world to Helsinki for what it billed as the "most epic dinner date".

Called Love at First Bite, the campaign aimed to bring strangers together over a candlelit dinner showcasing Finnish cuisine, with the possibility of finding love.

title: The type of homeowners on the rise as fewer Australians take out a mortgage
text:
in brief Australia saw the biggest drop in investor home loans on record in the September quarter.

A greater proportion of owner-occupiers are taking out mortgages.

Rising interest rates and Labor's tax changes have spurred the biggest drop in investor home loans on record, as owner-occupiers claim a greater share of the housing market.

New investor lending fell 30.6 per cent to 35,301 loans in the September quarter, driving a 15 per cent fall in total home loans, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported on Wednesday.

While lending to owner-occupiers also fell, the shallower 5.3 per cent decline meant the share of owner-occupiers taking out home loans has climbed to 68 per cent from 59 per cent before the May budget.

Labor has been wary of claiming all the credit for the deepening housing downturn, amid falling consumer and business confidence.

But Housing Minister Clare O'Neil said the rising share of owner-occupiers in the market was a good early indicator that the tax changes were having their intended effect.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"What we're seeing is that more first home buyers are winning auctions that they're competing in," she told Seven's Sunrise program.

"We've got a long way to go here, but we've got some important pieces of progress being made."

ABS head of finance statistics Mish Tan said lending activity fell across all borrower types, but the decline was sharpest for investors.

"Our data suggests that investor activity is being influenced by factors beyond increasing borrowing costs, including the potential impacts of tax changes and expectations of lower house prices," he said.

Loans taken out by first home buyers decreased 8.6 per cent during the quarter and were 12.3 per cent lower than a year prior.

But first home buyers still accounted for a "significant share of owner-occupier lending" at more than one-third, the ABS said.

Number of houses for sale on the rise

As buyers have shied away from the market, the number of homes for sale has soared in almost every capital city, contributing to an oversupply that is pushing prices down.

In Brisbane, total available stock was 24.4 per cent above the five-year average in the four weeks to November 8, according to property data firm Cotality.

The city's median dwelling value fell two per cent in October, the steepest fall in the country.

In Melbourne, the rate of decline slowed to 0.8 per cent, the shallowest fall among the five major markets.

In contrast to the rest of the country, the Victorian capital had 5.3 per cent less stock available for sale than its average.

"A better balance between available supply and demand in Melbourne means home values in the city are falling at the slowest pace of the major capitals," Cotality head of research Gerard Burg said.

Recovery in housing market 'unlikely' for now, expert says

Although total properties for sale were rising in most markets, new listings were actually slowing.

In Brisbane, new listings declined 12.4 per cent over the year, while the number of properties for sale increased 59.5 per cent.

The discrepancy is due to listings staying on the market longer.

In October, the median national property was on the market for 41 days, compared with 24 days a year earlier.

Signs of a recovery elsewhere remain a long way off.

READ MORE The Australian housing challenge not being solved

The Reserve Bank's latest rate rise — taking interest rates to an 18-year high — will further reduce buyers' purchasing power, and the government's tax changes continue to affect investor sentiment.

"A recovery in housing market conditions is unlikely until buyers have the confidence and financial capacity to return to the market," Burg said.

"Affordability and investor policies are likely to remain constraints, meaning rate cuts from the Reserve Bank will be necessary, which currently appears unlikely before the second half of 2027."

title: What's hidden beneath this Commonwealth Bank building is becoming more valuable
text:
In central Sydney, a 27-tonne vault door has stood guard for almost a century.

In October 1926, it took around 25 horses to move it from the wharf to its destination in Martin Place, where the rest of the building was constructed around it.

It's also one of the few still operated by a big bank.

Australian banks have reportedly closed hundreds of vaults alongside the closure of physical branches, with the costs of maintaining vaults becoming too expensive.

But as banks withdraw from the market, private operators are picking up their unwanted facilities.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

ABC Bullion is among companies that manage private vaults. General manager Jordan Eliseo the company has found demand demand had at least "doubled, if not tripled in the last decade".

Volatility in financial markets and higher inflation tend to stimulate higher demand for gold and precious metals.

"We had the global financial crisis 20 years ago. You had the European debt crisis about 15 years ago. You had Brexit. You had the pandemic, and then you had last year," he told SBS News.

One of the most ornate bank vaults sits underneath the Martin Place branch of Commonwealth Bank. Source: Supplied / Commonwealth Bank

"All of those all of those events have seen gold demand, and therefore demand for things like private vaults increased quite quite substantially."

Eliseo said there is strong demand in migrant communities, particularly those from China, India and Bangladesh.

"Consumers and households from those regions are typically quite friendly towards investing in gold. It's been a long trusted savings asset in those communities," he said.

There also tends to be higher usage of self-managed superannuation funds among these communities, according to Eliseo, where bullion can be used for retirement investment but may also require safe storage.

Westpac is the latest big bank to join ANZ and National Australia Bank in transitioning their vault services to private operators.

John Fleming, general manager at the Australian Security Industry Association, said it's a shift that allows banks to focus on their core services while private operators invest in vault offerings.

He said there has been "a lot of investment in these areas, and private people wouldn't invest in these areas if it wasn't a growth market".

As prices of precious metals like gold go up, Fleming said so does demand for ways to store them safely.

"People, even small homeowners who may have some jewellery at home who may not feel secure," he said.

"You can't put that in the cloud."

Items often stored in vault security include precious metals, diamonds, family heirlooms, hard drives and important legal documents.

Fleming said vault storage operators invest in thorough security measures.

"They put a lot of effort in, whether it's video surveillance, biometrics, on-site monitoring, or seismic detection through the wall, so that somebody from the outside trying to drill or make a hole in the wall gets picked up straight away," he said.

Common items stored in vaults include precious metals, family heirlooms and important documentation. Source: Supplied / Commonwealth Bank

While other big banks move away from these services, Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA) said it's a growing area for them.

CBA has 135,000 customers using safe custody vaults and have added around 32,000 new vaults over the last two years. Monica Wegner, CBA's executive general manager of everyday banking, said CBA experiences more demand around cultural festivals.

"We do see amongst our vault customers that about half of the vaults are occupied by migrants to Australia," she said.

"We observe people wanting to store things for different reasons," she said.

"Sometimes it's even natural disasters. You can imagine with things like fires, they don't want to have important documents at home. They want to have them in a safe space."

Wegner doesn't see demand shrinking any time soon.

"It's interesting because you might expect because other things are digitising, why would we still need these vaults?" she said.

"But at the end of the day, you still have customers that have things that are very precious to them."

Both Huang and Powell are married to other people.

The New York Times reported Huang had engaged in a second affair with one of his subordinates, Kimberly Powell, who is Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare. Nvidia’s code of conduct instructs staff to avoid situations that could create conflict, including “personal relationships”. Who is Lori Huang? The scandal also has ramifications for Huang’s personal life. Huang’s admission has fuelled speculation about the fate of his 41-year marriage with Lori Huang, 64. She is president of the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation, which had $US9 billion ($13.1 billion) in assets as of 2024, including $US6 billion in fresh funding that year. Of Jensen Huang’s 922 million Nvidia shares, more than half belong to a trust where he and Lori Huang are the co-trustees, according to financial filings. She is also the sole controller of a trust that owns about $US5 billion worth of Nvidia shares. Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, walk to the White House to attend a state dinner hosted for Chinese President Xi Jinping in September. AP Photo/Carolyn Kaster

Advertisement

Lori Huang joins a small group of tech titan spouses who have had to grapple with public infidelity. The list includes MacKenzie Scott, the ex-wife of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, and Melinda French Gates, ex-wife of Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates. The succession problem: who might replace Huang? Huang co-founded Nvidia back in 1993, and had led the company ever since, with no clear successor in sight. Huang’s ouster has led to a scramble for a new permanent chief executive, and Nvidia said it was considering both “internal and external candidates”. Donald Trump nominated former Apple chief Tim Cook as an ideal candidate to take over as Nvidia CEO. AP As well as Kress, various other names have been floated as potential successors, including Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky, Nvidia executive Ian Buck – credited as the tech genius behind the CUDA software that allows developers to write code on the company’s chips, AMD chief executive Lisa Su (who is a cousin of Jensen Huang), Arm boss Rene Haas, former Google chief Eric Schmidt and Intel chief executive Lip-Bu Tan. US President Donald Trump also weighed in, saying former Apple chief Tim Cook should take the role.

Advertisement

“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple,” Trump said on social media. “A Legend replaces a Legend!” he added. Where investigations stand Nvidia hasn’t provided any notable new updates in its internal review that was first announced at the weekend. At the time, the company said it had “no reason to believe” that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information. Trump was reportedly briefed about intelligence findings involving Huang well before the scandal erupted publicly. But when asked at the weekend whether he wished he had acted sooner on that information, the president said, “I don’t think so”, and maintained that Nvidia’s chief executive was an “honorable guy”. Loading

Advertisement

Trump later said the FBI was looking into Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, although where exactly that probe stands is unclear. Meanwhile, lawmakers from both sides of the aisle on Capitol Hill are calling for further investigations. Many eyes have been on Nvidia’s ties to Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which prominently touts the companies’ partnership on its website. Last year, Megaspeed was accused of illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China, but in December said there was “no evidence” of such exports. On Thursday, Megaspeed maintained that it took its obligation to comply with American export control laws “extremely seriously” – and that it was committed to working “constructively and transparently” with the US government. Singaporean authorities said they questioned Alice Huang and confiscated her passport last year as part of an investigation into Megaspeed. They concluded there wasn’t enough evidence that she had committed a crime, but suspected she provided “inaccurate information” to downplay her role at Megaspeed and barred her from returning to the country. China, meanwhile, has denied that it attempted to ensnare Jensen Huang. Its Foreign Ministry earlier this week called the spying allegations “unsubstantiated” and said they amount to a smear campaign.

Advertisement

What is it with the leather jackets? Jensen Huang has become known for his vast collection of leather jackets. They have become a staple of his wardrobe and his persona, and were his trademark look while delivering speeches. Huang credits wife Lori and daughter Madison with coming up with the look. He is reported to have 60 jackets in his wardrobe. A Tom Ford leather jacket worn and signed by Huang, sold in July at a Sotheby’s auction for $US960,000. The proceeds were donated to charity. Huang has become known for his leather jackets. AP Photo/John Locher

Advertisement

Donald and Jensen’s bromance Huang has maintained a close relationship to Trump throughout the Republican president’s second term in office. He has successfully lobbied for looser AI regulation overall – including less strict limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China. And he is among tech chief executives who have dined at the White House, and even travelled on Air Force One. Trump has called Huang “smart” and “amazing”, repeatedly insisting he join him on foreign trips. After news of his resignation broke on Thursday, the president maintained that Huang had done “done a fantastic job”. Huang and Donald Trump at the US Institute of Peace in Washington. AP

Advertisement

The entrepreneur praised Trump effusively in 2025 before a meeting. “I come with only one purpose only, which is to inform and to be in service of the president as he thinks about how to make America great,” Huang told reporters. Nvidia committed $US25 million to help fund Trump’s White House ballroom renovation, a major personal priority for the president in his second term. Last month, Trump presented Jensen Huang with the National Medal of Science. On Friday, Trump said Huang called him and expressed remorse over what the scandal had done to his family. Trump, in a White House interview with the broadcaster Stephen A. Smith on Thursday, praised Huang just hours after his ouster. “What he’s done is incredible,” Trump said. “Nvidia is unbelievable.

Advertisement

“I spoke to him yesterday. He’s going through hell. What he feels most badly about is his wife and family. That’s what he told me. He called me.” How has this affected Nvidia’s share price? Nvidia shares closed 4.3 per cent lower and have tumbled this week, wiping nearly $US500 billion off the market capitalisation of the company. The company is now valued around $US4 trillion, having been worth more than $US5.8 trillion in early October. Nvidia’s value has plummeted this week. Bloomberg Jensen Huang’s personal net worth has fallen by about $US19 billion this week, dropping him out of the world’s top 10 richest people list, according to Forbes. He is now the 13th richest person in the world with a net worth of about $US143 billion.

Advertisement

A new test for the AI industry The shockwaves of Huang’s exit stress just how few figures hold so much power in the AI race. Nvidia is one of the world’s most valuable companies today – and Huang has risen to fame across the tech world. Related Article Analysis

AI Jensen Huang once told me his two golden rules. He may have broken one of them Some analysts suspect that the foreign intelligence allegations will strengthen calls in Washington for stricter export controls with China, which could in turn renew trade strains overall. Others have called it a watershed moment for Nvidia, the chipmaker that has long been seen as the crown jewel for powering AI. And questions of security risks facing the companies at the forefront of this technology are piling up Stephanie Balaouras, group research director for Forrester, said Huang’s resignation from Nvidia wasn’t just a test for the company but the AI boom as a whole.

Advertisement

“If Nvidia stabilises quickly under new leadership, the AI infrastructure boom will have demonstrated resilience,” she said. “If its stock, financing relationships, or ecosystem commitments remain under sustained pressure, that would add evidence to the fragile side of the AI bubble ledger.” AP, Bloomberg The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. text:

SportRacingHorse racing Collett ready to help as ‘little family’ mourns Izzy Neale Craig Kerry November 13, 2026 — 5:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
