As one of the most experienced members of female jockeys’ rooms in Sydney and its surrounds, Alysha Collett tries to help out the growing number of apprentices whenever she can. It is support the 32-year-old group 1-winner feels was missing in the far sparser rooms when she was coming through the ranks. Jockey Alysha Collett. Getty Images And it is support needed more than ever this week after the heartbreaking death of Scone apprentice Izzy Neale. “It’s a little family in that jockeys’ room, and it’s honestly just devastating,” said Collett, who rides $5.50 favourite Sweynesday in the $1 million The Hunter on Saturday at Newcastle.

Advertisement

“It’s really unfair what’s happened, but the girls have all stuck together, which is really nice to see. “Izzy was just a lovely girl. It’s heartbreaking. Izzy Neale in July. Getty Images “Mikayla [Weir] and Maddy [Owen] and others, they were good friends with her. I don’t know what they would be going through right now. It’s brutal, and it’s a bit of reality, for what things can happen, for the young apprentices as well. That’s probably the tough thing to swallow also.” Neale’s family announced the 22-year-old’s death on Tuesday night, following a fall at Warren on Sunday when her mount Marnoo broke down on the home turn with a catastrophic injury.

Advertisement

It was the first race fall death of a jockey in NSW since Darren Jones in 2017 and has triggered an outpouring of grief and tributes for Neale, who had been riding professionally for less than three years. The tragedy has rocked the racing community, especially the huge group of female apprentices in NSW. Collett rides regularly at all levels and often makes herself available as an adviser in stewards inquiries, or mentor outside of them, for her younger colleagues. Female apprentices (back) Mollie Fitzgerald, Siena Grima, Olivia Chambers, Izzy Neale, Coriah Keatings, Rebecca Bronett Prag, (front) Anna Roper and Shannen Llewellyn at Rosehill on June 27. Getty Images “I want them to do well because when I was younger I never really had that help, so if I can help them in any way possible, I try to do it,” Collett said. “If they ever ask what did I think of that ride, or what could I have done different, we are all open for opinions and help, all us seniors, like Rachel [King] as well. It’s nice we are able to do that.”

Advertisement

Collett heads to Newcastle’s annual standalone on Saturday with the main job of riding winners, and she has strong chances in the day’s richest two races. She has picked up the ride on Annabel and Rob Archibald-trained Sweynesday in the Hunter. The six-year-old came from last to finish a close second to Ndola in the GH Mumm Rising Fast Stakes (1200m) two weeks ago at Flemington in what was his second start since coming from the Roger James and Robert Wellwood stable. He has drawn well in gate six for the 16-strong 1300m quality and Collett hoped to capitalise. “It’s a really open market, but we’ve drawn a good barrier,” she said. “His run the other day was brilliant in Melbourne. “I’ve ridden it once early doors, but he seems pretty straightforward.

Advertisement

“From the bad barrier in nine the other day over 1200m, they were a little bit sharp, so they looked to ride him where he was happy, but from the better barrier we might try to utilise that. We’ll have to talk about that. “There’s a good amount of pace in the race, which is nice. There’s a bit of pressure, which I think will fall into his lap nicely.” Collett also rides Todd Pollard-trained Zuleika ($6.50) in the $300,000 Beauford (2300m). She was aboard when the mare was third to Anthracite at Randwick over 1600m, before she was eighth last Saturday in the Matriarch (2000m) at Flemington. “I rode her two starts back and she went brilliant,” she said. “I’m excited to get back on her, over a 2300 set up, too. To me, if there was another 200m in that Randwick run, she would have just kept picking up and going, so I thought for a mile run, it was super.

Advertisement

“She’s got great tactical speed and she’s a great horse to ride because she goes forward and when you ask her to come back, she comes back and relaxes.” Maher getting Fawkner Park on track Declan Maher would do well to one-up his big brother, Ciaron, given the run the champion trainer is on. Tempted’s Everest win and a history-making Melbourne Cup trifecta have led a remarkable spring for the Victorian. Declan, though, can claim bragging rights, of sorts, if he can get veteran stayer Fawkner Park to fire in the $300,000 Beauford (2300m) on Saturday at Newcastle.

Advertisement

Fawkner Park, now eight, raced at a high level for the Annabel and Rob Archibald stable, winning the $1.2 million Q22 and placing three times in group 1s, before going to Ciaron Maher. After one poor run and two trials, the trainer convinced connections to send Fawkner Park to his brother’s new Gold Coast stable, which he established in April last year. Declan Maher (right) with Ciaron Maher and jockey William McCarthy. Getty Images “Ciaron just wasn’t completely happy with him and since I’d moved to Queensland, he’d met Kurt Gasky, my physio, and he had worked on a few Ciaron had sent up here,” Declan said. “He just thought he needed that regular maintenance.”

Advertisement

Fawkner Park, a $10 chance in the Beauford, is unplaced in seven starts since the move, but Declan feels he can challenge on Saturday after finishing four and a half lengths away over 1815m last week at Eagle Farm. “When I got him, he ran really well first up in the winter and then he got a little splint,” he said. “It muddled up that preparation a bit, so we reset. “I thought he ran really well first up, then I elected to leave him in Sydney and it was probably the wrong call. He requires a bit of maintenance with his body. Kurt does a lot with him to keep him free and moving at his best, so I got him home after that and he ran really well last Saturday. “It was more like an 1800m trial. They went slow in front and ran home quick. For where he was, and the weight he had, it was a big ask, but he bounced through the run and has been really fresh all week and I’ve been really keen to get him out to that trip on Saturday.

Advertisement

Declan Maher. Vicky Hughson “He’s got a bit of an enigma about him, that’s why I’ve had a few gears changes on him. An old gelding, you’ve got to keep him thinking a bit. “But his last 600 the other day was one of his best in a dozen starts. If he let go like he can, he’s right in it.” Declan, who has a team of 20, worked closely with Ciaron for many years before going out on his own, but the brothers still help each other out. Fawkner Park travelled to Ciaron’s Bobs Farm property on Thursday. “I’m still working indirectly with my brother,” he said.

Advertisement

“It’s good, and it’s also handy if we need to chew the fat over a few things. He’s a handy bloke to have a conversation with.” He hopes to take Fawkner Park to the Christmas Cup at Randwick on December 12, if he runs well on Saturday.

Australian Gold and Copper has delivered a spectacular polymetallic intersection from its Evergreen project in NSW’s highly endowed South Cobar basin, with a 16-metre drill hit returning 2.3 grams per tonne (g/t) gold, 70g/t silver, 1.4 per cent copper and a combined 12.2 per cent lead-zinc from 112m. The stunning reverse-circulation (RC) hole was sweetened by multiple high-grade zones, including a 6-metre core running at 5.2g/t gold, 157g/t silver and a combined 27.9 per cent lead-zinc from 116m. Adding to the intrigue was a separate, copper-rich two-metre kicker grading a hefty 6.2 per cent copper from 123m. Australian Gold and Copper’s Evergreen project in NSW, where recent drilling has returned high-grade polymetallic results. The same hole also produced a shallower intercept of 6m assaying 2g/t gold, 20g/t silver and 0.9 per cent copper from 84m, demonstrating multiple mineralised lenses over more than 220m of strike at the Hillston mineralised zone within Evergreen. Separately, the main Evergreen mineralised zone has been defined over more than 500m of strike. The results form part of the company’s drilling campaign, targeting the high-grade Western Discovery zone at the company’s South Cobar project, as it builds towards a maiden resource estimate for the Evergreen deposit. The standout hole was specifically targeted up-dip and south of a previous discovery hole that returned a 17-metre intercept grading 5.3g/t gold, confirming the system has legs.

Advertisement

′ The high-grade western discovery zone remains open along strike and at depth.′ Australian Gold and Copper managing director Glen Diemar Other notable assay results from the first 18 holes of the 21-hole, 2593-metre RC program add weight to the discovery, showing it is far from a one-hit wonder. One hole returned 9m running 1.6g/t gold and 58g/t silver from 90m, including a higher-grade 5-metre section going 2.4g/t gold and 94g/t silver. Nearby, a further interval yielded 6m grading 1.4g/t gold and 53g/t silver from 95m, featuring a one-metre section of 5.7g/t gold and 202g/t silver. Australian Gold and Copper also reported new assays from previously unsampled historical diamond drill core. A standout hit returned a 7-metre slice of 3.1g/t gold and 18g/t silver from 100m, including a 0.7-metre snippet at a solid 5.9g/t gold. The project sits within a sprawling 2600-square-kilometre landholding in a region known for its world-class deposits. Australian Gold and Copper managing director Glen Diemar said: “This is an exceptional hole. The combination of 6m at 5.2g/t gold, 157g/t silver, 1.0% copper and 27.9% lead-zinc, followed by a copper-rich interval of 2m at 6.2% copper, is an outstanding result at such shallow depths. The high-grade western discovery zone remains open along strike and at depth.” Australian Gold and Copper says its approach is to use broad-spaced drilling to establish the scale of the mineralised system before tightening its focus on the richest and widest zones. The strategy has already served the company well at its Achilles discovery, just 30km away, where an initial 38.5-million-ounce silver-equivalent resource was defined in 2024, with a hefty 58 per cent in the stronger indicated category.

Advertisement

With regulatory approvals now in hand for a third phase of drilling at Evergreen, the rods will be turning again later this quarter. Management says a higher-capacity RC rig is scheduled to arrive to test extensions to the high-grade zones it has just uncovered. In addition, an induced polarisation geophysics survey is underway at the nearby Mount B target, with results pending. Rounding out the portfolio, 230 km to the south, the company holds the Junee project, adding a pure-gold play to its growing stable of precious and base-metal assets. Notably, Australian Gold and Copper remains well-funded to continue its exploration push, with a healthy $5.9 million in cash and no debt as of the end of September. The Evergreen discovery is shaping up to be a significant one for the company. The latest volley of high-grade, polymetallic results from shallow depths confirms a robust mineralising system that appears to remain open along strike and at depth. With a maiden resource estimate for Evergreen on the horizon, assays from three RC holes still pending and a bigger rig on its way to chase the system deeper, Australian Gold and Copper looks likely to give punters plenty of newsflow to watch out for. Bulls N’ Bears Big Hits looks at notable drill intercepts reported this week to the ASX. Junior explorers have put on a clinic in how to deliver both sheer grade and massive vertical scale this week, proving that standout drill results can come from everything from a happy geotechnical outcome to deep, multi-horizon sulphide systems. From shallow bonanza gold grades in the Top End and towering porphyry copper columns in southern Peru, through to stacked platinum group metal reefs in WA’s remote West Musgrave, their drill bits have been working overtime across the globe. So let’s dive in. FAR NORTHERN RESOURCES LIMITED (ASX: FNR) Project: Bridge Creek gold project, Northern Territory

Hit: 4m at 110.06g/t gold from 16m downhole Drilling a hole purely for metallurgical and geotechnical testing, only to stumble onto a blistering, shallow bonanza gold zone, is the kind of serendipity every junior explorer dreams about. Far Northern Resources has pulled off that exact coup with one of six diamond drill holes put into its Bridge Creek project, 125 kilometres south-southeast of Darwin in the Northern Territory.

Advertisement

Targeting the northwestern margin of its Bridge Creek Central deposit, where previous drilling had been sparse, the company’s headline hole bored into a high-grade shoot just 16 metres below surface. The intercept returned a remarkable 4-metre length of core grading 110.06 grams per tonne (g/t) gold, underpinned by an eye-watering single-metre chunk assaying 425.2g/t gold from 16m. That’s “thirteen-and-a-half-ounce dirt” in the old prospectors’ language. Immediately above that bonanza zone, the same hole tagged 2m at 14.14g/t gold from 11m, before hitting further mineralised runs of 2m at 1.14g/t gold from 30m and 3m at 3.05g/t gold from 36m. Clocking in at a 440 gram-metre comparative index, the company says that primary intercept is the best one drilled at Bridge Creek to date. And while ground conditions forced the hole to be abandoned at 68.9m, it still gave a last hurrah with 0.9m at 0.83g/t gold from 68m. While the northwestern margin delivered the high-grade fireworks, a second diamond hole pierced straight through the heart of the central deposit to highlight its bulk scale, returning a whopping 60-metre intercept grading 2.0g/t gold from 53m, marking the longest continuous mineralised interval ever drilled at Bridge Creek. Not only did it break the intercept-length record, its broad run was also laced with multiple internal zones, including 7m at 4.13g/t gold from 53m and 28m at 2.10g/t gold from 69m, featuring several single-metre spikes up to 16.41g/t gold.

Advertisement

Situated along the tightly folded axis of the Howley Anticline, roughly 12km north of the historic Cosmopolitan Howley gold mine, the mineralisation sits within quartz-sulphide stockwork zones hosted by black shales and altered dolerites. The latest assays from the six-hole, 584.3-metre diamond campaign will feed straight into a resource upgrade slated for early 2027. Bridge Creek currently hosts 93,000 ounces of gold, forming the backbone of the company’s 117,000-ounce Northern Territory resource base, alongside its nearby Ios project. With the bonanza shoot remaining wide open to the northwest, along strike and down-dip, Far Northern is gearing up for repeat and screen fire assaying on the high-grade core while also planning immediate follow-up drilling ahead of a scoping study later next year. Diamond drill core from AusQuest Limited’s headline hole at the Cangallo project in Peru showing vibrant blue-green oxide chrysocolla and malachite copper mineralisation between 156m and 164m downhole. AUSQUEST LIMITED (ASX: AQD)

Advertisement

Project: Cangallo porphyry copper-gold project, Peru

Hit: 618m at 0.26% copper and 0.06g/t gold from 36m downhole Proving up sheer vertical scale across an emerging porphyry system is the name of the game in South America, and AusQuest Limited has delivered in spades after tagging more than 600 metres of continuous copper-gold mineralisation at its Cangallo project in southern Peru. Positioned 25 kilometres east of the coastal town of Chala, the company’s latest diamond drilling campaign set out to test the depth extent of stockwork veining in the northern sector of the company’s wholly owned prospect. The headline diamond hole stole the show, boring through copper mineralisation from just 36 metres downhole to return a massive 618m run grading 0.26 per cent copper and 0.06g/t gold. That broad envelope was bolstered by several punchier internal intervals, led by a shallow 114-metre zone assaying 0.40 per cent copper and 0.07g/t gold from 88m, alongside deeper hits of 26m at 0.41 per cent copper from 254m and 30m at 0.41 per cent copper from 438m.

Advertisement

A second diamond hole backed up the scale narrative by intersecting an even longer 708-metre zone grading 0.21 per cent copper and 0.05g/t gold from just 4m below surface. It also featured a higher-grade shallow core of 40m going 0.40 per cent copper and 0.11g/t gold from 28m. Other sweeteners in the second hole included 14m assaying 0.35 per cent copper and 0.08g/t gold from 280m; 20m going 0.35 per cent copper and 0.08g/t gold from 438m and 14m running at 0.33 per cent copper and 0.08g/t gold from 538m depth. According to management, the two holes represent the longest copper intercepts reported at Cangallo to date. The most significant copper intercepts across all six holes were accompanied by gold responses up to 0.14g/t, silver to 1.6g/t and molybdenum to 120 parts per million. Interestingly, the system showcases two distinct styles of copper mineralisation. The first is a shallow supergene oxide blanket extending to almost 250m depth, carrying typical secondary-zone chrysocolla and malachite copper mineralisation.

Advertisement

That shallow zone transitions into deeper primary zone stockwork veins loaded with the distinctive copper-iron- sulphide minerals chalcopyrite and bornite, both of which are key ore minerals for copper. Geological mapping indicates the multi-phase intrusive system spans at least 1.5km of strike, with associated dykes stretching beyond 2.5km and remaining wide open. Notably, momentum is also building for the company on the regulatory front, with the Peruvian Government recently declaring Cangallo a project of national interest - a development the company expects will streamline future permitting. With environmental and community approvals already locked in for 20 new drill pads, AusQuest is preparing to mobilise rigs for a stage four reverse circulation program later in the year to test strong surface copper and gold anomalies in the south. TERRA METALS LIMITED (ASX: TM1)

Project: Dante project, Southwest prospect, Western Australia

Advertisement

Hit: 67m at 2.07g/t 3E and 0.13% nickel from 332m downhole Threading a single diamond hole through four stacked mineralised zones while banking project-record platinum group metal grades is a serious statement of intent. Terra Metals has just pulled off that feat at its Southwest discovery in Western Australia’s remote West Musgrave region, where deep drilling continues to unlock a sprawling magmatic sulphide system. Within the company’s wholly owned, 3000-square-kilometre Dante project, the headline diamond hole was designed to test the central block of the Southwest prospect at depth. The hole delivered a standout run of 67m grading 2.07g/t platinum, palladium and gold and 0.13 per cent nickel from 332m downhole. That broad envelope encased an intensely mineralised 31.9-metre zone averaging 3.96g/t platinum, palladium and gold, 0.23 per cent nickel and 0.12 per cent copper from 366m. Boring deeper into the structural reef system revealed even hotter internal spikes, including 8.9m at 11.85g/t platinum, palladium and gold and 0.54 per cent nickel from 389m, including 0.9m assaying 15.86g/t platinum, palladium and gold, 1.84% nickel, 0.13 per cent cobalt and 0.18 per cent copper from 390.4m.

Advertisement

That same 31.9m zone also included 4.7m going 17.90g/t platinum, palladium and gold, 0.36 per cent nickel, 0.19 per cent copper from 393.15m. In a resounding crescendo at 396.8m depth, the drill core delivered a blistering, project record bonanza zone of 1.1m assaying 72.71g/t platinum, palladium and gold - or 2.34 ounces to the tonne - with 0.33 per cent copper and 0.27 per cent nickel. Not to be suppressed too early after that previous headline act, the same hole also intersected three additional mineralised horizons across an eye-watering 452m of drilling, proving that the stacked, near-surface architecture noted in the east plunges cleanly through the central corridor. Above the main zone, the drill bit chewed through a 97.8-metre zone going 1.18g/t platinum, palladium and gold, 0.13 per cent copper and 0.17 per cent nickel from 225.2m, while a deeper slice hit 21m at 1.02g/t platinum, palladium and gold from 520m, including 0.93m at 8.92g/t platinum, palladium and gold and 2.02 per cent nickel. Geologically, the Southwest prospect sits within the Giles Intrusive Complex, with local faulting helping to concentrate high-grade massive and semi-massive sulphides. It lies in the same layered mafic-ultramafic belt that hosts BHP’s massive Nebo-Babel deposit, a magmatic nickel-copper-PGE sulphide system, containing a massive combined 390 million tonne resource grading 0.30 per cent nickel and 0.33 per cent copper. With four drills still at work and more than 35,000m of drill samples from Southwest sitting in the laboratory pipeline, Terra is backed by a hefty $57.9 million cash war chest. Its metallurgical results are due this quarter, ahead of a maiden resource estimate for Southwest early next year and a scoping study slated for mid-year towards a potential prefeasibility study. PoliticsFederalBig four Like taxing blood donors: Bank boss reveals biggest gripe Shane Wright November 13, 2026 — 4:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The head of one of the nation’s largest banks has likened state payroll taxes to “taxing people who give blood” in a full-throated plea to the nation’s politicians to slash red tape and government spending. But the chief executive of Australia’s biggest home lender, Matt Comyn, has cautioned borrowers that interest rates will remain higher as the world deals with the AI construction boom, geopolitical disruption and economic shocks that seem to be accelerating in number. NAB chief executive Andrew Irvine. Alex Ellinghausen NAB boss Andrew Irvine and Comyn gave evidence on Friday to a parliamentary hearing into the banking sector that has been dominated by the state of the economy, government spending and the housing market. The British-Canadian Irvine, who took over as the head of the NAB in 2024, said he continued to be stunned that a country as large as Australia with a population of less than 30 million could have a housing crisis.

Advertisement

“It’s honestly like we’re playing poker with a handful of aces and we’re losing. How is that possible? I find it so disappointing,” he said. Irvine said the level of regulation across the country, especially when it came to construction, was way too high. He then turned his attention to the tax system, particularly state payroll taxes. “[It’s] the most atrocious, abominable tax. It would be like taxing people who give blood,” he said. Irvine said that in the early 2000s, government spending as a share of the economy was a “world-class” 23 per cent. Now it was around 29 per cent which, while lower than most nations, has grown strongly under both sides of politics.

Advertisement

Related Article Big four Cut government spending to reduce inflation: Big banks’ plea He said lower spending, which Treasurer Jim Chalmers has signalled will form a part of his mid-year budget update next month, would take pressure off inflation and interest rates while allowing the private sector to grow. “It is undoubtedly true that additional public sector spending, in an environment where we have poor productive supply capacity, is unhelpful,” Irvine said. “Public spending in and of itself is crowding out private sector spending and that is problematic. I would point out it’s not just the federal government, it’s all levels of government, state government, local councils, it’s everything.” Comyn noted that lower government spending would reduce inflation pressures across the country, but warned it would not be a panacea for all the issues facing Australia.

Advertisement

He said the surge in spending in areas such as AI meant the very low interest rates of the 2010s – when the cash rate in Australia fell to 0.75 per cent ahead of the pandemic – were gone. “The outlook for interest rates is higher than it has been for the past decade,” he said. Comyn said while Australian government debt – which on Friday fell below $1 trillion – was much lower than most other nations, it was important for fiscal discipline. CBA chief executive Matt Comyn says shocks to the global economy are growing in number. Alex Ellinghausen He said a suite of policy reforms were needed to boost productivity which would then help Australia deal with an increasingly shock-prone global economy that was straining under pressures stretching from the AI construction boom to demographic change to geopolitical tensions.

Advertisement

“I think the structural forces that are shaping geopolitics make it far less predictable,” he said. Related Article Negative gearing Record plunge in investor loans as tax overhaul hits property market “Living within your means as a company and country is important … there are much more significant and more frequent shocks likely to affect the economy.” Comyn also suggested the Reserve Bank, which has lifted the cash rate five times this year, may have erred in cutting interest rates last year, saying it could have waited longer to ensure inflation was going to stay within its 2-3 per cent target band before easing monetary policy. Westpac’s chief economist, Luci Ellis, on Friday said the RBA may be done with interest rate rises as the economy slows more quickly than anticipated by the Reserve.

Advertisement

She said the fallout from this year’s steep fall in house prices would weigh on the broader economy and inflation well into next year. The recent drop in oil prices, which are now below what the RBA forecast only a week ago, would also aid in reducing price pressures across Australia. “[Monetary] policy is clearly restrictive, and the risk of overdoing the inflation correction is growing,” she said. Markets opened with a spring in their step this week, only to finish flat on their backs again. Oil took the first hit as hopes of an end to the war in Iran sent barrel prices tumbling from around US$100 to below US$90 for the first time since August...that’s before President Donald Trump grabbed the brake lever on Thursday, shouting “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed.” This week’s Bulls N’ Bears Runner of the Week is… G8 Education. The orange leader of the free world continued, stating that the US had hundreds of billions of dollars of frozen overseas Iranian regime money and that the US in fact controlled the Strait. The Brent price suggested otherwise, bouncing back to almost US$96 in a serious rollercoaster of a week. Inflation fears were quick to follow as hot US cost-of-living data mixed with oil had the punters betting on a December Fed rate hike, leaving bond yields uncomfortably close to five per cent and the US dollar surging once again. Gold, in turn, handed last week’s rally straight back, slipping below US$4000 and shedding nearly three per cent overnight to around US$3880.

Advertisement

Bad news flowing from the Middle East left AI as the last shiny hope and for a few days, Wall Street delivered. Fresh from last week’s US$3.2 trillion rout, tech roared back. Then Jensen Huang’s wandering eyes got involved. Nvidia’s chief admitted an extramarital affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, prompting the board to investigate whether he had been the “target of a foreign intelligence effort”. Reports linked the woman to Megaspeed, Nvidia’s biggest Southeast Asian customer, which was already accused of “chip smuggling.” The world’s biggest company proceeded to shed more than US$427 billion (A$627 billion) in two sessions - the most expensive affair since Helen of Troy. Then came Wednesday night’s twist: The New York Times reported a second alleged affair, this time with a senior Nvidia executive, while The Wall Street Journal said the board was preparing to show him the door. By Thursday, a reported third dalliance had emerged, and shares in the world’s biggest company were down 20 per cent in a little over a week… oooft.

Advertisement

Back home, everyday Australians continue to feel the hurt, with consumer sentiment at a four-year low, rates at an 18-year high and mortgage holders’ mood plunging alongside their housing prices. And the reward for all that government-induced inflation? A parade of praise for Dr Jim Chalmers. With calls for his resignation growing louder, Labour lined up to slap him on the back. Albo declared the Treasurer was “doing a great job” – at raising revenues - and that he wanted him by his side. Standing by your man is a fine quality in a mate, but not when it’s at the cost of tens of millions of people across the country, I’d wager. Meanwhile, Usman Khawaja was busy standing by his Australian cricketing brethren in a different way this week. Waiting beside them at the bus stop to throw his old teammates under the wheels, it seems, for a more personal form of revenue raising in his latest autobiography. His claim that ‘Sandpapergate’ went well beyond the three players who were banned was a great way to honour the Baggy Green, with his dirty gossip rag – biography – set to hit shelves just in time for Christmas. Finally, the market mayhem week looked like it might come to an end, only for Australians to wake Friday morning to Microsoft’s entire office offering on the fritz, with Outlook and Teams remaining down throughout the business day. Business was at a standstill, with nowhere more evident than the market overlords down at the ASX, who certainly didn’t have the answers. Outlook’s outage sent the ASX’s archaic system scrambling, as a grand total of just 180 announcements made it out on Friday, a fraction of the usual 550ish daily haul.

Advertisement

Last week it was fridges frying; this week it’s Outlook dying - and the consequences of a major technology outage are flooding across the market. The ASX was again down another one per cent on Friday’s reduced traffic, which left this week’s Runners paddling against the current. Not a single stock managed to crack the 100 per cent gain mark, although with the small-cap tide running so rough, staying afloat for our four Runners this week counts for something. G8 Education operates more than 350 early learning and childcare centres across Australia. G8 EDUCATION LIMITED (ASX: GEM) Up 95% (10.5c – 20.5c) Bulls N’ Bears Runner of the Week is G8 Education, after the childcare heavyweight landed a $196.7 million takeover proposal at 26c per share from Melbourne investment manager Majority Capital Partners, sending its battered share price soaring.

Advertisement

The non-binding offer represented a whopping 160 per cent premium to G8’s previous close of 10 cents, putting a very different value on a business the market had been treating like yesterday’s lunch. Majority Capital has lined up bank and equity commitment letters covering the full consideration, while G8 has signed a process deed giving the suitor up to six weeks of exclusivity to complete due diligence and negotiate a binding deal. G8 says it operates more than 350 early learning and childcare centres across Australia under a stable of established brands, making it one of the country’s biggest providers of early childhood education and care. The business has been operating in a tough environment, with cost pressures, staffing challenges and regulatory scrutiny weighing on the childcare sector. The approach is also part of a broader takeover stir in the education sector. Just a day earlier, international education provider IDP Education revealed it had received a revised $3-a-share proposal from private equity giant Blackstone, valuing the business at about $834 million.

Advertisement

Blackstone had previously tabled offers of $2.30 and $2.50 a share, both rejected, before returning with a 20 per cent sweeter bid as IDP shares continued to languish. The two approaches in as many days suggest private equity is sniffing around a sector that public markets have perhaps punished too heavily. CLARITY PHARMACEUTICALS LIMITED (ASX: CU6) Up 57% ($1.50 - $2.35) Slotting into second and scoring a major regulatory win this week was Clarity Pharmaceuticals, after the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted the Aussie hopeful “Breakthrough Therapy ” status for its copper-64 imaging agent, 64Cu-SAR-bisPSMA, used to detect post-treatment prostate cancer. The technology helps doctors find recurring cancer, even when conventional scans struggle to show exactly where it is hiding. It works by seeking out a protein commonly found on prostate cancer cells, effectively lighting them up so they can be spotted on a PET scan.

Advertisement

The scan is particularly important for men whose blood tests show rising levels of PSA, a protein that can signal prostate cancer has returned, sometimes before doctors can pinpoint the location of the disease. The FDA designation is a significant regulatory leg-up and gives Clarity closer access to senior FDA officials, more intensive guidance and a potentially faster pathway through the development and review process. It is also the first time the agency has granted Breakthrough Therapy status to a PSMA-based PET imaging agent. The clinical numbers are also turning heads. In the Co-PSMA study, Clarity’s imaging agent detected cancer in 78 per cent of patients, compared with just 36 per cent using an existing gallium-68 imaging agent in the same patient group. In other words, it found cancer in more than twice as many patients, potentially giving doctors a much better picture of where the disease has returned and how best to treat it. Clarity now has two major Phase III trials, AMPLIFY and CLARIFY, fully recruited, with patients being monitored ahead of topline results expected in the first half of next year, suggesting the 57 per cent jump on this week’s news could be just the start of a very busy financial year to come. CARNEGIE CLEAN ENERGY LIMITED (ASX: CCE)

Advertisement

Up 57% (14c – 22c) Carnegie Clean Energy surfed a hefty share-price wave this week, climbing 57 per cent on no news to the market whatsoever. It seems the company’s next-generation CETO wave energy technology and its looming offshore demonstration in Spain may have been the ticket. Carnegie released a detailed presentation, setting out how it plans to prove its wave energy technology can make the leap from promising engineering concept to commercially viable power generation business. The CETO demonstrator is destined for the Biscay Marine Energy Platform off Spain’s Basque coast. Unlike conventional wave-energy devices bobbing around on the ocean surface, CETO operates fully submerged, using the movement of an underwater buoy driven by passing waves to power a system that converts that motion into electricity. Keeping the machinery below the surface is designed to improve storm survivability, reduce visual impact and sidestep some of the community opposition that has dogged offshore wind projects. ‘ACHIEVE’ is intended to test six key parts of the technology in real ocean conditions, from energy capture and AI-enabled control systems to extreme-weather survivability, reliability and maintenance.

Advertisement

The company says CETO’s modular design should make it easier to manufacture, transport and install using existing industrial supply chains and smaller vessels. Carnegie says it is targeting commercial capacity factors of 30 to 50 per cent at suitable wave-energy sites, alongside forecast energy density of 30MW per square kilometre - five times the typical figure cited for offshore wind. With shares surging this week, Carnegie has plenty of wind in its sails. The ACHIEVE demonstration is the next big test, with European backing already secured and a much larger 6MW CETO array on the drawing board. Capability X’s CX remote is a portable, ruggedised remote operations system that enables the control and monitoring of remotely operated vehicles (ROV’s), unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV’s) and robotic systems technology. Capability X Limited (ASX: CX8)

Advertisement

up 55% (20c – 31c) Rounding out our Runners was AI-driven industrial safety developer Capability X, after the newcomer made a cracking ASX debut this week, surging as much as 55 per cent above its 20-cent IPO price to hit 31 cents on Thursday. The $12 million float arrived as investors grow increasingly choosy about AI valuations; however, Capability X is offering something more tangible than another chatbot with billion-dollar dreams - technology already working in industrial environments, backed by paying customers and recurring contracts. Its platform combines cameras, laser sensors, lidar and proprietary AI software to build a real-time, three-dimensional picture of busy industrial sites. The company says it identifies workers, vehicles and machinery, tracks their movements and flags dangerous interactions before they turn into accidents. Rather than simply recording incidents, the system is designed to spot trouble brewing and alert operators before someone gets hurt.

Advertisement

The technology has already attracted customers across marine, ports, logistics and offshore operations. ASX-listed Bhagwan Marine has signed a multi-year agreement, logistics heavyweight Qube Ports has committed to a three-year rollout of CX Protect and offshore operator GO Offshore has also adopted its safety systems. Multi-year hardware and software leases provide a recurring revenue stream rather than relying on one-off equipment sales. Beyond workplace safety, the platform could help industrial operators lift productivity, reduce downtime and operating costs, with mining and defence offering obvious expansion opportunities as remote operations become increasingly important. With solid revenues and a growing suite of customers already under its belt, Capability X is looking to take its industrial AI platform into a much bigger arena. In a world drowning in AI promises, this tech looks to be already earning its keep. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
